title: Acid–Base, Electrolytes, AKI & Renal Support
note: Set 5: Learn chapters (Acid–Base, Electrolytes, AKI & Renal Support notes, structured for easy reading), learning outcomes, landmark trials and a linked reading list. Speak, Retrieve and SAQ content to follow.

items.title: 1. Acid–base physiology and the disciplined interpretation of blood gases
items.body:
## 1.1 Why pH matters: what a measured hydrogen ion concentration represents

- The hydrogen ion activity of arterial blood is tightly defended at a pH around 7.35–7.45 despite continual production of CO₂ and fixed metabolic acids. pH is logarithmic: a fall from 7.40 to 7.10 represents approximately a **doubling of hydrogen ion concentration**, not a small numerical shift.
- Acidaemia depresses myocardial contractility and catecholamine responsiveness, promotes pulmonary vasoconstriction, can contribute to arrhythmias and changes the distribution of potassium.
- Alkalaemia promotes cerebral and coronary vasoconstriction, lowers ionised calcium by increasing albumin binding and facilitates arrhythmias in the setting of potassium and magnesium depletion.

The intracellular environment is buffered by proteins and phosphates; haemoglobin buffers hydrogen ions generated in red cells as CO₂ enters. The **bicarbonate–carbon dioxide system** is clinically special because each component can be controlled by a different organ. In conventional units, the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation is:

**pH = 6.1 + log₁₀ [HCO₃⁻ / (0.03 × PaCO₂ in mmHg)].**

The relationship is a ratio: pH falls when bicarbonate decreases or PaCO₂ increases. The lungs adjust alveolar ventilation over minutes, whereas kidney responses to changes in bicarbonate reclamation, ammonia generation and titratable acid excretion take hours to days. A blood-gas value must therefore be understood in the context of **when** the disturbance arose.

- PaCO₂ is related to CO₂ production and alveolar ventilation, not simply minute ventilation: PaCO₂ ≈ (0.863 × V̇CO₂)/V̇A when compatible units are used.
- Dead space increases the minute ventilation required to achieve a given PaCO₂.
- This is why a shocked patient with pulmonary embolism may have a high respiratory rate yet become hypercapnic despite an apparently large minute ventilation.

- The normal kidneys filter a very large bicarbonate load, reclaim almost all of it mainly in the proximal tubule, and generate new bicarbonate by net acid excretion.
- Ammoniagenesis from glutamine is especially important as a sustained response to acidosis.
- Acute kidney injury impairs net acid excretion and may cause an increased-anion-gap acidosis once retained acids accumulate.
- Kidney failure can also cause a non-anion-gap acidosis through inadequate ammonium excretion, particularly before retention of unmeasured anions is marked.

## 1.2 What blood-gas analysers actually measure—and what they calculate

- Arterial analysers directly measure **pH, PaCO₂ and PaO₂**, usually by electrochemical electrodes.
- Bicarbonate on a standard blood-gas printout is **calculated from pH and PaCO₂**; it is not an independently measured value.
- Standard base excess (SBE) is also derived: it estimates the amount of strong base required to titrate blood/extracellular fluid back to a standard pH at PaCO₂ 40 mmHg and therefore helps isolate the metabolic contribution.
- SBE is not a diagnosis: it can be influenced by chronic respiratory adaptation, significant hypoalbuminaemia and other changes.
- SpO₂ and calculated SaO₂ are not equivalent to **measured co-oximetric oxygen saturation**, which is necessary to diagnose dyshemoglobinaemia.

- Venous blood gases are highly useful for pH, bicarbonate, lactate, many electrolytes and trending metabolic treatment, but **venous PO₂ must not be used to infer arterial oxygenation**.
- Venous pH is generally a little lower and PCO₂ a little higher than arterial; differences become unpredictable in low-flow shock, regional hypoperfusion or major ventilation–perfusion abnormalities.
- If precise PaCO₂ affects a ventilator decision, severe mixed disorder or cerebral blood-flow target, obtain an arterial sample.
- A critical-care venous gas can answer an acid–base question while a simultaneous arterial gas answers the oxygenation question.
- The 2025.1 Final specifically examined the utility of VBG measurement.

- The sample can mislead.
- Delayed analysis after collection allows cellular metabolism to alter gas values
- Air bubbles increase or decrease PO₂ toward room-air conditions and tend to reduce PCO₂
- Excess liquid heparin can dilute electrolytes
- Flush contamination distorts sodium, chloride, glucose and potassium
- And marked leukocytosis may produce pseudo-hypoxaemia through ongoing oxygen consumption.
- Compare any surprising result with the patient’s examination, sample source and the laboratory biochemical panel.

## 1.3 An interpretation sequence that finds mixed disorders

**Step 1: Decide whether the patient is acidemic or alkalemic.** A pH below 7.35 is acidaemia and above 7.45 is alkalaemia. A normal pH does not exclude a severe mixed process: opposing metabolic and respiratory disturbances can cancel on the pH line. Very severe acidemia (often pH <7.1–7.2) or alkalemia (>7.55) demands urgent physiological assessment, not merely a label.

**Step 2: Identify the primary direction:**

- Low bicarbonate contributes to metabolic acidosis; high bicarbonate to metabolic alkalosis.
- High PaCO₂ contributes to respiratory acidosis; low PaCO₂ to respiratory alkalosis.
- Compare with the pH and clinical timing.
- A patient with pH 7.25, bicarbonate 12 and PaCO₂ 26 has primarily metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation.
- A patient with pH 7.25, bicarbonate 30 and PaCO₂ 68 has primary respiratory acidosis, despite a high bicarbonate value.

**Step 3: Test whether compensation is plausible.** Compensation is usually incomplete. A value outside the expected range is a separate primary disorder until proven otherwise; do not call it ‘over-compensation’.

| **Primary process** | **Expected physiological response** | **Interpretation trap** |
|---|---|---|
| Metabolic acidosis | **Winter’s formula:** expected PaCO₂ = 1.5 × HCO₃⁻ + 8 (±2 mmHg) | Higher PaCO₂ means additional respiratory acidosis; lower means additional respiratory alkalosis |
| Metabolic alkalosis | PaCO₂ ≈ 40 + 0.7 × (HCO₃⁻ − 24) (±5 mmHg) | Excessive hypoventilation suggests sedative effect, COPD or fatigue |
| Acute respiratory acidosis | HCO₃⁻ increases ≈1 mmol/L for each PaCO₂ rise of 10 mmHg above 40 | Elevated bicarbonate alone is not a second alkalosis |
| Chronic respiratory acidosis | HCO₃⁻ increases ≈3.5–4 mmol/L per 10 mmHg PaCO₂ rise | A sudden fall in PaCO₂ can cause post-hypercapnic metabolic alkalosis |
| Acute respiratory alkalosis | HCO₃⁻ falls ≈2 mmol/L for each PaCO₂ fall of 10 mmHg | Common in acute PE and sepsis |
| Chronic respiratory alkalosis | HCO₃⁻ falls ≈4–5 mmol/L per 10 mmHg PaCO₂ fall | Typical of sustained pregnancy hyperventilation or chronic liver disease |

- The responses are approximations, less reliable at extremes and in evolving disease.
- Example: HCO₃⁻ 10 mmol/L predicts PaCO₂ 23 ±2.
- If measured PaCO₂ is 40, a dangerous **superimposed respiratory acidosis** is present even if the ventilator displays apparently adequate respiratory rate.
- The patient may be unable to maintain the high alveolar ventilation that the original metabolic acidosis demanded.

- **Step 4: Calculate the anion gap (AG) for every metabolic acidosis.** AG = Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻) in mmol/L, often quoted around 8–12 when potassium is omitted; use the laboratory reference range.
- Albumin is the major normal unmeasured anion.
- Correct AG for hypoalbuminaemia: **AG corrected ≈ AG measured + 2.5 × (40 − albumin g/L)/10**.
- Thus an observed AG of 12 with albumin 20 g/L corrects to about 17, which may indicate otherwise hidden accumulation of lactate or other unmeasured acids.
- A ‘normal AG’ in a severely hypoalbuminaemic ICU patient is not necessarily reassuring.

- **Step 5: Ask why the anion gap is high—or why chloride has replaced bicarbonate.** A high corrected AG suggests lactate, ketones, uraemic anions, toxins or selected rare organic acids.
- A normal-gap (hyperchloraemic) metabolic acidosis reflects loss of bicarbonate or impaired acid secretion with relative chloride excess: diarrhoea, high-volume saline, pancreatic or intestinal drainage, renal tubular acidosis, and some phases of renal insufficiency.
- Both mechanisms can coexist.

- **Step 6: Identify additional metabolic disorders when the AG is high.** Calculate ΔAG = measured/albumin-corrected AG − normal AG, and ΔHCO₃⁻ = 24 − measured HCO₃⁻.
- The ΔAG/ΔHCO₃⁻ ratio is often called the **delta ratio**.
- Roughly <0.8 suggests coexisting normal-gap acidosis; around 1–2 is compatible with high-gap acidosis; >2 suggests a superimposed metabolic alkalosis or pre-existing elevated bicarbonate.
- Interpret against baseline CO₂ retention, albumin and the particular acid; rigid numeric cutoffs are unreliable in complex ICU cases.

- **Step 7: Link the acid–base diagnosis to oxygenation, perfusion, renal function and a cause.** Do not stop after a formula.
- Re-examine lactate, ketones, glucose, electrolytes, creatinine, medications, temperature, sepsis/ischemia and the ventilation waveform.
- Calculate the alveolar oxygen gradient if hypoxaemia is a question: PAO₂ ≈ FiO₂ × (PB − 47) − PaCO₂/0.8 (sea-level approximation).
- An increased A–a gradient implies V/Q mismatch, shunt or diffusion limitation, not isolated hypoventilation.

**Mixed metabolic disorders:**

- An albumin-corrected anion gap can identify an additional metabolic process even when a patient has an apparently plausible compensatory PaCO₂.
- For a raised gap, calculate ΔAG = corrected AG − the local upper limit of normal (often around 12 mmol/L when potassium is omitted), and compare it with ΔHCO₃⁻ = 24 − measured bicarbonate.
- A ΔAG/ΔHCO₃⁻ ratio substantially below 1 suggests additional normal-gap metabolic acidosis; above about 2 suggests concomitant metabolic alkalosis (or pre-existing high bicarbonate).
- These are screening estimates, not independent diagnoses: the ratio is unreliable when bicarbonate is near normal, albumin and anion-gap reference ranges are uncertain, or mixed time courses are present.
- The important exam skill is to explain how vomiting, chloride loading and keto/lactic acid accumulation can coexist and to state what you would measure next.

**Blood gases in critical illness: what to trust:**

- Compare the measured bicarbonate from serum chemistry with the calculated gas bicarbonate if results are surprising.
- Compare the arterial PaCO₂–end-tidal CO₂ difference: a widening gradient may indicate increasing dead space, falling pulmonary perfusion or equipment/sampling problems, not necessarily a fall in CO₂ production.
- A venous sample can help follow metabolic recovery, but profound shock makes the arterial–venous PCO₂ gap variable and may give misleading reassurance about ventilation.
- Reconcile any calculated acid–base category with respiratory pattern, inspired oxygen, lactate, albumin, ketones and renal function.
- The BJA Education 2023 review of metabolic alkalosis and mixed acid–base disturbance is particularly useful for analysing overlapping chloride, albumin and respiratory processes.

## 1.4 Worked examples that demonstrate clinical reasoning

**Example A: pH 7.01, PaCO₂ 50, HCO₃⁻ 12.2 mmol/L:**

- There is severe acidaemia and low bicarbonate indicating metabolic acidosis.
- Winter predicts PaCO₂ ≈ 26 mmHg; measured PaCO₂ of 50 is far higher, so there is a life-threatening **mixed metabolic and respiratory acidosis**.
- Potential causes include severe shock with exhausted respiratory effort, intoxication causing respiratory depression and tissue hypoperfusion, or ventilator failure during severe lactic acidosis.
- Prioritise ventilation, perfusion and identification of the metabolic source.
- This resembles a 2019.1 examiner question.

- **Example B: pH 7.49, PaCO₂ 29, HCO₃⁻ 22.6, PaO₂ 56 on room air.** Primary respiratory alkalosis predominates.
- For an acute fall in PaCO₂ of 11, expected bicarbonate is about 22, so compensation is appropriate.
- However PaO₂ 56 represents significant hypoxaemia.
- PAO₂ ≈ 150 − (29/0.8) = 114, producing an A–a gradient around 58 mmHg: consider pneumonia, pulmonary embolism, hepatopulmonary syndrome, interstitial disease or shunt rather than assuming hyperventilation explains the hypoxaemia.
- This is the framework tested in the 2020.2 report.

- **Example C: chloride 115, sodium 140, bicarbonate 14, albumin 18 and lactate 4.5.** Observed AG = 11, seemingly normal; albumin correction adds 5.5, revealing a corrected AG about 16.5.
- Both lactate accumulation and chloride-related (or gastrointestinal/renal) bicarbonate loss may be present.
- Fluids containing high chloride can obscure the raised-gap pattern.
- Restoring oxygen delivery, reducing unnecessary chloride, treating any ongoing gut loss and following serial measurements is more useful than naming a single ‘normal-gap’ diagnosis.

## 1.5 The physicochemical (Stewart) approach and why it can clarify the conventional model

- The physicochemical model treats pH and bicarbonate as **dependent variables** governed by three independent variables: PaCO₂, the strong-ion difference (SID), and the total concentration of non-volatile weak acids (Atot, mainly albumin and phosphate).
- Simplified plasma apparent SID is (Na⁺ + K⁺ + Ca²⁺ + Mg²⁺) − (Cl⁻ + lactate⁻).
- A fall in SID, commonly caused by a chloride rise relative to sodium or an increase in lactate, produces a metabolic acidifying effect.
- A decrease in albumin produces metabolic alkalinisation because albumin is a weak acid.

- This model is helpful in the ICU because saline-induced hyperchloraemic acidosis, mixed acid disturbances and the alkalinising effect of hypoalbuminaemia may appear paradoxical in a bicarbonate-only narrative.
- For example, 0.9% saline has a strong-ion difference of approximately zero, lower than plasma: administering large volumes can reduce plasma SID and bicarbonate.
- Lactated Ringer’s and Plasma-Lyte contain metabolizable anions and lower chloride loads, so their effective SID differs after metabolism.
- Importantly the Stewart and traditional models describe the **same chemistry** and should converge on clinically consistent conclusions, not compete for different diagnoses.
- See BJA Education’s [2022 acid–base physiology review](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2022.06.003), [2022 acid–base quantification review](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2022.07.006), and [2024 metabolic acidosis review](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2023.12.005).

items.title: 2. Acid–base emergencies in shock, anaesthesia and critical care

items.body:
## 2.1 Shock disrupts both acid production and effective carbon dioxide elimination

- Shock is inadequate effective tissue perfusion and/or oxygen utilisation relative to metabolic demand.
- When mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation is impaired, pyruvate may be converted to lactate; but lactate also rises with adrenergic stimulation, reduced hepatic clearance, impaired pyruvate handling and some drugs.
- A raised lactate is a **signal to evaluate the whole perfusion–metabolic state**, not proof of pure anaerobic metabolism.
- Reassess the trajectory with capillary refill, skin perfusion, mental status, echocardiography, blood pressure, urine output, haemoglobin, oxygenation, infection and medications.

- **Early shock can produce respiratory alkalosis** as chemoreceptors respond to hypoxaemia, fever, pain, catecholamines and metabolic acidosis.
- When fatigue, severe lung disease or sedative-induced hypoventilation develops, PaCO₂ may normalise or rise.
- A patient with severe metabolic acidosis who suddenly has a ‘normal’ PaCO₂ may be deteriorating: the expected PaCO₂ should have been markedly low.
- Sepsis can therefore cause lactic acidosis plus respiratory alkalosis, while cardiac arrest or terminal shock more often creates combined respiratory and metabolic acidosis.

- Lactate alone should not dictate fluids.
- High lactate may reflect sympathetic drive, seizures, β₂ agonists, metformin-associated toxicity in appropriate contexts, mesenteric/ischaemic injury or liver failure.
- A high lactate with good skin perfusion, preserved circulation and substantial adrenaline exposure has a different interpretation from high lactate with worsening mottling, low cardiac output, abdominal pain and oliguria.

## 2.2 Metabolic acidosis: categorise mechanisms before giving bicarbonate

- The most clinically useful mechanisms are **new acid accumulation**, **bicarbonate loss**, and **failure to excrete acid**.
- Lactic acidosis is often driven by tissue perfusion–oxygen delivery mismatch, although type B causes are also important
- Diabetic, alcoholic and starvation ketoacidosis reflect insulin deficiency/low carbohydrate availability and hepatic ketogenesis
- Kidney injury limits acid excretion
- Gastrointestinal losses or saline cause relatively normal-gap acidosis.
- Rare poisonings—methanol (formate), ethylene glycol (glycolate), salicylates and metformin-associated lactic acidosis—require early toxicology support and sometimes extracorporeal clearance.

- The clinical effects depend on pH, tempo, calcium and potassium status, and the degree of underlying cardiovascular disease.
- Severe acidaemia impairs catecholamine response, promotes pulmonary arterial vasoconstriction and may decrease myocardial contractility.
- Acidosis may also be compensatory in severe tissue hypoperfusion: normalising a laboratory number without restoring circulation does not correct the underlying defect.

**Treat the cause first:**

- Re-establish effective perfusion and oxygen delivery, treat infection/ischemia, stop precipitating drugs, supply insulin for ketoacidosis, replace bicarbonate-rich gastrointestinal losses, optimise ventilation and assess dialysis triggers.
- Correct measured glucose, sodium, potassium and ionised calcium concurrently.
- Avoid automatically increasing minute ventilation to ‘normalise’ PaCO₂ in every acidotic patient; differentiate true compensation from inappropriate hyperventilation and balance lung protection against the need to preserve respiratory compensation.

**When bicarbonate may be appropriate:**

- In severe acidemia with significant AKI or haemodynamic instability, sodium bicarbonate may temporarily improve pH and sometimes defer KRT, but does not consistently improve survival.
- Bicarbonate generates CO₂: without adequate alveolar ventilation, CO₂ enters cells readily and can aggravate intracellular or CSF acidosis.
- Other harms are sodium load, fluid expansion, decreased ionised calcium, hypokalaemia, alkalosis and overshoot.
- It is more physiologically compelling in bicarbonate loss (for example renal tubular acidosis or high-output enteric loss) than in untreated ketoacidosis or ongoing lactate production.
- The [BICARICU-2 trial (2025)](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2025.20231) enrolled patients with pH ≤7.20 and moderate/severe AKI: bicarbonate **did not reduce 90-day mortality** (approximately 62% in each group), although KRT use was lower (35% vs 50%).
- These outcomes should prevent both an absolute ‘never give bicarbonate’ rule and an equally misleading claim of survival benefit.

**SODa-BIC (2026):**

- Bicarbonate for shock with metabolic acidosis, not necessarily severe AKI.
- In this double-blind, placebo-controlled, pragmatic trial, 500 ICU patients receiving vasopressors were enrolled across 55 ICUs in seven countries.
- Eligibility required pH <7.30, base excess ≤−4 mmol/L and PaCO₂ ≤45 mmHg if not intubated (≤50 mmHg if intubated).
- Unlike BICARICU-2, moderate–severe AKI was not a prerequisite.
- Patients received a protocolised sodium bicarbonate infusion or 5% glucose placebo for up to five hours, titrated towards pH ≥7.30 and base excess ≥0 mmol/L.
- The 30-day composite of death, RRT or persistent renal dysfunction (MAKE30) occurred in 40.2% versus 39.4% (adjusted difference 1.2 percentage points; 95% CI −7.1 to 9.4; P=0.78).
- RRT occurred in 16.8% versus 20.9%, and day-30 in-hospital mortality in 25.4% versus 24.0%; neither difference demonstrated a reliable benefit.
- This is evidence against routine bicarbonate solely to improve renal or survival outcomes in a broad vasopressor-treated acidotic population, not evidence that bicarbonate is never indicated.

**Putting the trials together:**

- In BICARICU-2, patients had more severe acidaemia (pH ≤7.20) plus moderate–severe AKI, and bicarbonate decreased RRT use (35% versus 50%) without changing 90-day mortality.
- SODa-BIC enrolled a broader shock population at pH <7.30 and showed no improvement in its blinded 30-day major adverse kidney outcome.
- The trials differ in eligibility, treatment protocols, blinding and outcomes; their results should not be pooled as though they tested an identical indication.
- A Bayesian meta-analysis published in November 2026 (four RCTs, 1544 patients) found no clear short-term mortality effect (RR 0.94, 95% credible interval 0.73–1.22) but suggested less RRT initiation (RR 0.74, 95% credible interval 0.59–0.98).
- RRT initiation may also be influenced by correction of a dialysis trigger, so fewer RRT starts do not automatically establish improved survival or long-term kidney recovery.

For ANZCA Final practice:

- Treat the cause.
- Assess severity, ventilation, potassium, volume status and AKI.
- Consider bicarbonate selectively for marked acidemia or bicarbonate loss, and do not delay indicated RRT.

## 2.3 Respiratory acidosis: think alveolar ventilation, dead space and mechanics

- Respiratory acidosis reflects CO₂ retention from inadequate effective alveolar ventilation.
- Causes include opioid/sedative overdose, neuromuscular weakness, airway obstruction, COPD/asthma, obesity hypoventilation, ventilator disconnection or inadequate settings, and high physiologic dead space.
- Immediate assessment is not just a gas result: evaluate airway patency, chest rise, work of breathing, ventilator waveforms, capnography, endotracheal tube position, circuit integrity, auto-PEEP and dynamic hyperinflation.
- Capnography may underestimate PaCO₂ substantially during shock/PE because dead space rises and expired CO₂ becomes less representative of arterial CO₂.

- Chronic hypercapnia is buffered by renal bicarbonate retention over days.
- If such a patient is abruptly ventilated to PaCO₂ 40 while bicarbonate remains elevated, a marked **post-hypercapnic metabolic alkalosis** may develop.
- In COPD or chronic respiratory failure, aim at physiological gas exchange, consciousness and haemodynamics rather than an arbitrary normal PaCO₂; protect against excessive tidal volume, dynamic hyperinflation and worsening auto-PEEP.
- Severe hypercapnia can raise intracranial pressure and pulmonary vascular resistance, requiring special caution in neurocritical care and pulmonary hypertension.

## 2.4 Respiratory alkalosis: do not reflexively sedate the patient

- Respiratory alkalosis reflects excessive alveolar ventilation relative to CO₂ production.
- Distinguish anxiety or pain from hypoxaemia, pneumonia, pulmonary embolism, sepsis, pregnancy, hepatic failure, salicylate toxicity and iatrogenic hyperventilation.
- In the shocked patient, abrupt disappearance of compensatory hyperventilation may herald ventilatory failure.
- Treat the cause; correct unnecessary ventilator respiratory rate or excessive tidal volume; and recognise symptoms such as paraesthesia, light-headedness, carpopedal spasm and reduced ionised calcium.
- Acute hypocapnia constricts cerebral vessels, explaining why deliberate hyperventilation is generally avoided outside short-term rescue of impending herniation.

## 2.5 Metabolic alkalosis: chloride, potassium and the kidney’s capacity to excrete bicarbonate

- Metabolic alkalosis begins with a **generation** process (loss of H⁺ in vomiting or nasogastric suction; diuretics and contraction alkalosis; exogenous alkali; post-hypercapnia) and persists through **maintenance** mechanisms: low effective arterial volume, chloride depletion, hypokalaemia, mineralocorticoid activity or kidney failure.
- Vomiting removes gastric HCl, while alkalosis persists because the kidney avidly reabsorbs NaCl and bicarbonate when volume and chloride are depleted.
- This is why the treatment is not simply ‘give hydrogen ions’.

- Urinary chloride is more informative than urinary sodium in many cases.
- **Urine Cl⁻ <10–20 mmol/L** generally supports chloride-responsive states such as vomiting, remote diuretic exposure or volume contraction; **>20 mmol/L** suggests persistent diuretic action, mineralocorticoid excess, severe potassium deficiency or selected tubulopathies (interpret with fluids and ongoing medications).
- In chloride-responsive alkalosis, replace saline or a chloride-containing crystalloid when appropriate, **replace KCl and Mg**, and stop gastric/diuretic losses.
- If fluid overload prevents saline, consider adjusting diuretics, acetazolamide for selected cases, or renal replacement therapy when severe and refractory.
- In mineralocorticoid-driven disease, address aldosterone excess and use appropriate antagonists.
- Severe alkalemia reduces cerebral perfusion and may cause ventricular arrhythmias, seizures and difficult ventilator weaning.

**When metabolic alkalosis is severe or refractory:**

- A patient with chloride-resistant alkalosis needs a deliberate search for mineralocorticoid excess, ongoing loop/thiazide exposure, Bartter/Gitelman physiology or exogenous alkali rather than repeated saline boluses.
- Assess BP, effective arterial volume, K/Mg, urinary chloride interpreted against recent fluids/diuretics, and potassium replacement needs.
- In an overloaded ICU patient receiving ongoing diuresis, acetazolamide can increase renal bicarbonate excretion, but may worsen hypokalaemia and requires renal-function assessment; it is not definitive treatment for an untreated driver.
- KRT with a tailored bicarbonate bath can be considered for life-threatening refractory alkalosis when kidney function or fluid status prevents conventional correction.
- Treat the physiological cause and monitor ECG, ionised calcium, potassium and serial pH rather than aiming for immediate biochemical normality.

## 2.6 The ventilated patient with profound metabolic acidosis: a peri-induction trap

- A patient with DKA, salicylate toxicity or septic lactic acidosis may maintain life-compatible pH by generating extreme spontaneous minute ventilation.
- Induction, apnoea and paralysis **remove that compensation immediately:** PaCO₂ rises rapidly, pH falls and circulatory collapse may follow.
- Anticipate high required alveolar ventilation, preoxygenate effectively, minimise apnoea, and match a safe but sufficient minute ventilation promptly after intubation; confirm with arterial gas rather than ETCO₂ alone.
- In severe obstructive lung disease, ventilation goals compete with dynamic hyperinflation, so optimise the cause and seek expert airway/ICU support.
- The safest plan may be to improve circulation and metabolic drivers before inducing anaesthesia when surgery is not immediately essential.

**Perioperative threshold thinking:**

- A single bicarbonate or pH value is not a universal cancellation threshold.
- An unstable patient with severe acidosis or hyperkalaemia needs treatment, optimisation or urgent surgery with resuscitation as required; an elective patient with unexplained significant metabolic derangement needs an explanation before anaesthesia.
- Consider severity, trend, cause, procedure urgency and capacity for postoperative ICU support.

items.title: 3. Sodium, tonicity and water balance—from physiology to neurological emergencies
items.priority: P1 CORE (3 parent LOs) + P3 MODERATE (2 parent LOs)
items.body:
## 3.1 Sodium is primarily a marker of water balance, not total body sodium content

- Serum sodium approximates the ratio of exchangeable Na⁺ plus K⁺ to total body water.
- A low sodium does not necessarily mean salt depletion, and high sodium generally means a **water deficit relative to exchangeable cations**.
- Water shifts rapidly across cell membranes to equalise tonicity, so plasma sodium disorders are brain-cell volume disorders.
- When extracellular fluid becomes hypotonic, water enters brain cells and may cause cerebral oedema.
- When extracellular fluid becomes hypertonic, brain cells shrink and adapt by accumulating intracellular electrolytes and osmolytes.
- The adaptation explains the opposing hazards: rapid deterioration in acute hyponatraemia and osmotic demyelination during overly rapid correction of chronic hyponatraemia.

- Arginine vasopressin (AVP, previously ADH) is released in response to hyperosmolality and, importantly, to non-osmotic stimuli such as pain, nausea, hypovolaemia, surgery, opiates and hypotension.
- AVP binds collecting-duct V₂ receptors, inserts aquaporin-2 water channels and permits free-water retention.
- Thirst is the companion protective response.
- Thus a postoperative patient receiving hypotonic maintenance fluid with nausea and ongoing AVP may rapidly become hyponatraemic, even if the administered sodium amount seems reasonable.

**Distinguish osmolality from tonicity:**

- Measured plasma osmolality includes urea and ethanol, which cross membranes relatively freely; effective osmolality (tonicity) excludes urea.
- In SI units, calculated plasma osmolality ≈ 2 × Na + glucose + urea (all mmol/L), while effective osmolality ≈ 2 × Na + glucose.
- Osmolal gap = measured − calculated osmolality; a substantial gap can suggest ethanol, toxic alcohols or unmeasured osmoles but is not diagnostic alone.
- Hyperglycaemia raises extracellular tonicity, pulls water from cells, and lowers the measured sodium by dilution even though total body water is often profoundly depleted.

- For hyperglycaemia, calculate a **corrected sodium**.
- A commonly used estimate adds approximately 1.6 mmol/L to measured Na for every 5.6 mmol/L increase in glucose above 5.6 mmol/L; at marked hyperglycaemia the relationship may be closer to 2.4 mmol/L per 5.6 mmol/L glucose increment.
- It is an estimate, not a target or replacement for serial measured sodium and calculated osmolality.
- Never diagnose true hypotonic hyponatraemia until serum osmolality/glucose are considered.
- Hyperlipidaemia and paraproteinaemia can cause pseudohyponatraemia with indirect ion-selective electrode methods; a direct blood-gas sodium and measured osmolality clarify this artefact.

## 3.2 Hyponatraemia: classify tonicity, then assess symptoms and water handling

- Hyponatraemia is sodium <135 mmol/L.
- Common clinical categories are **hypotonic**, hypertonic/translocational (usually glucose) and isotonic/pseudohyponatraemia.
- Hypotonic hyponatraemia is the clinically important brain-swelling disorder.
- Define acute onset as clearly <48 hours and chronic as ≥48 hours or unknown; assume chronic when onset is unclear because rapid correction may be dangerous.

- A useful diagnostic sequence is to check plasma osmolality, then **urine osmolality**, then urinary sodium interpreted alongside volume status, medications and cortisol/thyroid function.
- Urine osmolality ≤100 mOsm/kg indicates relatively suppressed AVP (primary polydipsia, low solute intake such as beer potomania).
- Urine osmolality >100 implies water retention through AVP or another renal water-handling problem.
- A low urinary sodium, often ≤30 mmol/L, may indicate low effective arterial volume; higher values occur in SIAD, diuretics, adrenal insufficiency, renal salt wasting and intrinsic kidney disease.
- Recent diuretic use, renal impairment and acute fluid treatment can invalidate simple cutoffs.

- Hyponatraemia in hypovolaemia arises because volume-dependent AVP release overrides the normal osmotic suppression; replace isotonic fluid and treat the cause.
- In heart failure and cirrhosis, total extracellular water and sodium are increased but **effective arterial circulating volume** is perceived as low, driving AVP and water retention.
- SIAD produces inappropriate renal water conservation despite non-hypovolaemic physiology, classically with concentrated urine and raised urinary sodium after excluding adrenal and thyroid deficiency.
- Neurological injury can produce SIAD or cerebral salt wasting; the latter is true sodium/volume depletion, and inappropriate fluid restriction can worsen cerebral perfusion.

- Symptoms depend more on the rate of change than sodium alone.
- Nausea, headache, gait disturbance and mild confusion may progress to seizures, reduced consciousness, brainstem herniation and respiratory arrest in acute severe hypotonic hyponatraemia.
- Recent neurosurgery, female sex, hypoxaemia and postoperative AVP may increase vulnerability to brain oedema.
- Always check glucose, sodium trend and concurrent hypokalaemia, which increases osmotic demyelination risk during correction.

## 3.3 Emergency treatment of severe symptomatic hypotonic hyponatraemia

- **Convulsions, severe encephalopathy or impending herniation demand prompt controlled elevation of sodium**, not routine slow correction.
- Give **3% sodium chloride 100–150 mL IV over 10–20 minutes** (institution-specific protocols differ), reassess symptoms and sodium, and repeat as needed to achieve an initial rise of approximately **4–6 mmol/L**.
- The intention is to reverse cerebral oedema, not make sodium normal.
- Manage airway and seizures simultaneously.
- Frequent serum sodium (often every 2–4 h, more often during active boluses) and urine-output monitoring are essential; sudden brisk water diuresis often predicts overcorrection.

- For established chronic/unknown-duration hyponatraemia, a conservative approach is to limit correction to **≤8 mmol/L in 24 hours** in those at high risk of osmotic demyelination (very low starting sodium, alcoholism, malnutrition, hypokalaemia, advanced liver disease); many clinicians use this ceiling broadly rather than relying on historically higher absolute limits.
- If the sodium is rising too quickly, stop active correction, assess aquaresis, and consider **desmopressin to clamp urine water loss**, often with D5W to relower sodium in consultation with renal/endocrine/ICU teams.
- KCl replacement itself increases effective cations and can raise serum sodium—count it in the correction trajectory.
- Some protocols deliberately use scheduled desmopressin early in high-risk patients to prevent unpredictable overcorrection.

- After stabilising neurologic symptoms, treat the cause.
- Hypovolaemic hyponatraemia needs isotonic rehydration with careful surveillance, because restoring volume suppresses AVP and may trigger rapid sodium rise.
- SIAD often needs fluid restriction and treatment of the pulmonary/CNS/drug cause; consider solute therapy, loop diuretics or specialist-guided vasopressin antagonists where appropriate.
- Vaptans are **not** the treatment for acute severe symptomatic hyponatraemia and can cause dangerous aquaresis.
- Hypotonic fluids should not be given indiscriminately during surgery to patients with ongoing AVP secretion.

**Preventing neurological injury from sodium overcorrection:**

- A sodium trajectory can accelerate dramatically once a hypovolaemic patient is resuscitated and non-osmotic AVP secretion switches off: urine may suddenly become very dilute and urine output high even without additional hypertonic saline.
- Urinary output and osmolality therefore provide early warning before a scheduled blood test reveals an excessive rise.
- In a patient at high risk of osmotic demyelination, frequent sodium checks and a specialist-directed desmopressin strategy may prevent this overshoot; a commonly used reactive dose is 1–2 micrograms IV/subcutaneously, with any further dose and D5W replacement guided by the observed sodium and urine response.
- Do not give D5W or desmopressin mechanically: symptomatic brain swelling, ongoing seizures and haemodynamic deficits require simultaneous assessment.
- Very low starting sodium, malnutrition, alcoholism, hypokalaemia and advanced liver disease warrant especially conservative correction ceilings.
- The initial 4–6 mmol/L rise used to reverse severe symptoms is part of the 24-hour total, not additional to it.

## 3.4 Hypernatraemia: why thirst, free-water access and kidney concentrating ability matter

- Hypernatraemia is sodium >145 mmol/L and indicates hypertonicity.
- In a conscious adult with intact thirst and access to water, sustained severe hypernatraemia is uncommon.
- It should therefore prompt questions about reduced consciousness, inability to drink, postoperative dysphagia, enteral feeding without sufficient water, fever/diarrhoea, osmotic diuresis, hypertonic sodium administration or diabetes insipidus (arginine vasopressin deficiency or resistance).

- Neurological signs are lethargy, confusion, irritability, neuromuscular excitability, seizures and sometimes intracranial haemorrhage from brain-volume contraction.
- Chronic hypernatraemia allows brain adaptation; overly rapid lowering may then provoke cerebral oedema.
- The water deficit can be approximated as **TBW × [(measured Na/140) − 1]**, using TBW ≈ 0.6 × body weight in a young man, 0.5 in many women/older men and less in frailty.
- This estimate excludes ongoing losses and should guide rather than dictate prescriptions.

**Preoperative/critical care sequence:**

- If haemodynamically shocked, first restore intravascular volume with an isotonic crystalloid; then replace free water enterally or with IV D5W/hypotonic fluid as indicated.
- For chronic/unknown-duration hypernatraemia, a common clinical target is a gradual fall around **≤10–12 mmol/L per 24 hours**, although adult evidence is less firm than for hyponatraemia and emergency stabilisation must be individualised.
- Calculate and re-check the sodium after treatment starts; account for fever, diarrhoea, polyuria, renal function and exogenous sodium.
- In true acute sodium loading, more rapid correction may be justified under specialist monitoring.

## 3.5 Polyuria, diabetes insipidus and neuroanaesthetic practice

- Polyuria after craniotomy or brain injury may be due to excess fluid administration, hyperglycaemic osmotic diuresis, diuretics, mannitol, hypertonic saline, recovery from AKI, cerebral salt wasting or **arginine vasopressin deficiency (AVP-D; formerly central diabetes insipidus)**.
- In AVP-D, hypothalamic/posterior pituitary damage impairs AVP release; kidneys cannot concentrate urine despite hypertonic plasma.
- Look for sustained high urine output (often >200–300 mL/h in adults or >2–3 mL/kg/h), increasing serum sodium/osmolality, inappropriately dilute urine (e.g., osmolality <300 mOsm/kg, often much lower), thirst if awake and falling volume status.

- AVP resistance (formerly nephrogenic diabetes insipidus) occurs with lithium exposure, hypercalcaemia, hypokalaemia, tubulointerstitial disease and hereditary receptor or channel abnormalities.
- A response to desmopressin helps distinguish deficiency from resistance but formal tests require endocrine oversight.
- Do not treat every postoperative high urine output with desmopressin; first determine whether urine is dilute or solute-rich and whether sodium is rising.

- If AVP-D is strongly suspected, replace circulating volume appropriately, calculate free-water needs and administer **desmopressin**, commonly IV **1–2 micrograms** for an acutely unwell adult with specialist guidance (dose and interval tailored to response), while monitoring hourly fluid balance, sodium and urine concentration.
- Excessive desmopressin plus free water can abruptly produce hyponatraemia.
- In haemodynamically unstable patients with AVP deficiency, vasopressin infusion may provide both antidiuretic and vasopressor action when appropriate.
- This is an examinable intraoperative topic in the 2025.1 Final report.
- In neurocritical care, avoid both dehydration-induced secondary brain injury and uncontrolled free-water replacement that worsens intracranial swelling.

**Intraoperative AVP-deficiency practical plan:**

- Before induction in a patient with known central AVP deficiency, identify their usual desmopressin route and last dose, ensure the medication is available in theatre, and write a fluid/urine/sodium monitoring plan.
- Loss of the intranasal/oral route, including fasting or nasal surgery, can precipitate a large dilute diuresis.
- For suspected acute postoperative deficiency, paired blood/urine osmolality and sodium trends distinguish hypotonic water loss from mannitol- or glucose-driven osmotic diuresis.
- The Society for Endocrinology provides adult rescue desmopressin doses of approximately 1–2 micrograms IV/IM, then recommends waiting for a return of large volumes of dilute urine before repeating in a decompensated patient to avoid over-treatment.
- Replace true intravascular volume depletion with suitable isotonic fluid first and then replace the free-water deficit and continuing losses; reassess frequently because a transient post-pituitary disturbance can evolve into water retention and hyponatraemia.

## 3.6 Perioperative application: the patient with severe dysnatraemia

**Preoperative:**

- Determine onset, symptoms, tonicity, current fluid balance and precipitant; review thiazides, SSRIs, antiepileptics, diuretics, desmopressin and enteral/IV water.
- Seek objective sodium trends and consider cortisol deficiency.
- Severe symptomatic hyponatraemia is treated before non-essential elective surgery; urgent procedures require explicit cerebral, airway and fluid planning.
- Chronic stable abnormalities are different from rapidly changing sodium values even at the same concentration.

**Intraoperative:**

- Avoid inadvertently worsening tonicity through large volumes of free-water-containing maintenance fluid or sodium-rich hypertonic products
- Monitor blood gases/electrolytes during prolonged surgery and massive transfusion
- Address nausea, pain and hypotension because they stimulate AVP.
- In patients with AVP-D, continue planned hormonal replacement and give water under close sodium surveillance.
- Preserve effective circulating volume and avoid hypotension.

- **Postoperative:** monitor sodium trends, urine output, symptoms, fluid inputs including enteral feeds, urinary losses and dextrose infusions. A patient whose chronic hyponatraemia corrects rapidly after the cause resolves may be at greatest risk **after** the procedure, particularly if aquaresis begins in PACU or ICU.

items.title: 4. Potassium, calcium, magnesium, phosphate and glucose emergencies
items.priority: P1 CORE (3 parent LOs) + P3 MODERATE (1 parent LO) + P5 MINIMUM (1 parent LO)
items.body:
## 4.1 Potassium physiology: concentration is not total-body content

- Almost all potassium is intracellular (approximately 98%); the narrow extracellular concentration of about **3.5–5.0 mmol/L** is maintained by cellular Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase activity, insulin and β₂-adrenergic activity, together with renal excretion in the distal nephron.
- Aldosterone promotes potassium secretion via the principal cells, and distal sodium delivery and tubular flow are needed for effective kaliuresis.
- Therefore two independent questions must be asked when potassium is abnormal: **has K shifted between cells and plasma, or has total body K changed?** Both can occur simultaneously.

- Insulin deficiency, metabolic acidosis (especially mineral metabolic acidosis), hypertonicity and tissue breakdown raise extracellular K even when total body stores are depleted.
- Diuretics, vomiting with secondary hyperaldosteronism, diarrhoea, insulin, β agonists and alkalosis lower plasma K, sometimes precipitously.
- A haemolysed sample, excessive tourniquet/fist clenching, extreme thrombocytosis or leukocytosis can cause pseudohyperkalaemia: repeat an appropriate sample if the clinical picture is inconsistent, but do not delay emergency treatment for ECG abnormalities.

## 4.2 Hyperkalaemia: treat electrical instability immediately, then remove potassium

**Why it kills:**

- Elevated extracellular potassium makes the resting membrane potential less negative.
- Initial repolarisation effects may cause peaked T waves, but progressive sodium-channel inactivation slows conduction: PR prolongation, flattened P waves, QRS widening, ventricular arrhythmias and asystole may follow.
- The ECG is **not reliably sensitive**; a dangerous concentration can coexist with modest changes, especially in chronic kidney disease.
- Risk is amplified by rapid rise, acidaemia, hypocalcaemia and structural heart disease.
- Severe hyperkalaemia is often treated as **K ≥6.5 mmol/L**, or lower if rapid rise, symptoms or ECG/conduction changes occur.

**Act in three physiologically distinct steps:**

- (1) **Stabilise the cardiac membrane.** For serious ECG changes, haemodynamic instability or hyperkalaemic arrest, give IV calcium.
- Typical adult arrest guidance is **10 mL of 10% calcium chloride** (preferably central/secure access; 6.8 mmol Ca²⁺), or **30 mL of 10% calcium gluconate** (approximately equivalent calcium) when appropriate.
- Monitor ECG and repeat calcium if electrical changes persist.
- Calcium acts within minutes but **does not lower potassium**.
- Avoid extravasation and check line compatibility.
- (2) **Shift K into cells.** Give short-acting insulin IV with glucose, classically **10 units insulin plus 25 g glucose** (adjust for baseline glucose, renal failure and local hypoglycaemia-prevention protocol); add nebulised **salbutamol 10–20 mg**.
- Recheck glucose frequently for at least several hours, because delayed hypoglycaemia is common in renal failure.
- Bicarbonate is not a reliable routine shift agent; reserve for concomitant significant metabolic acidosis or specified resuscitation circumstances.
- (3) **Remove K.** Stop sources, assess urine flow, use loop diuretics if effective volume status and kidney function permit, consider potassium-binding medicines for non-immediate elimination, and obtain **urgent dialysis** for refractory severe hyperkalaemia, renal failure or repeated rebound.

A concrete sequence in theatre:

- Stop suspected potassium infusion/transfusion source.
- Call for help.
- Obtain ECG/ABG and confirm specimen validity without delaying treatment.
- Give calcium for ECG changes.
- Give insulin/glucose and adjunct β₂ agonist.
- Correct severe acidemia when indicated.
- Call renal/ICU for KRT if K remains high or the patient is anuric.
- Sample K after ≈30–60 minutes and anticipate rebound at 2–3 hours.

- **Suxamethonium should be avoided** with significant hyperkalaemia and with conditions that upregulate extrajunctional ACh receptors (major burns after the initial period, denervation and many neuromuscular disorders).
- Balanced crystalloids with 4–5 mmol/L K are not automatically contraindicated in all hyperkalaemic patients; acid–base effects and volume indications also matter.

- The [2026 ANZCOR guideline for resuscitation in special circumstances](https://www.anzcor.org/home/adult-advanced-life-support/guideline-11-10-resuscitation-in-special-circumstances) recommends in hyperkalaemic cardiac arrest: calcium chloride 10% 10 mL rapidly (or calcium gluconate 10% 30 mL), insulin 10 units plus glucose 25 g, and **50 mmol bicarbonate** when severe acidosis/renal failure, while considering dialysis for refractory arrest.
- This specific cardiac-arrest recommendation must not be confused with advice against **routine bicarbonate** for uncomplicated acute hyperkalaemia.
- The [October 2026 Australian Prescriber review](https://australianprescriber.tg.org.au/articles/management-of-acute-hyperkalaemia-evidence-practice-and-pitfalls.html) and [2026 BMJ review](https://www.bmj.com/content/394/bmj-2026-100287) provide detailed evidence and pitfalls.

- **Why potassium treatment is not finished after the first normal measurement.** Insulin and nebulised beta-agonists redistribute K but do not remove it, so rebound can follow within hours as the pharmacological effect fades.
- Repeat serum K roughly 1 hour after treatment and continue serial monitoring at 2–4 hours or as clinically indicated; follow glucose for at least 6 hours after insulin–glucose, with particular vigilance in CKD, low baseline glucose and poor intake.
- A normal ECG never excludes severe hyperkalaemia.
- If severe ECG changes coexist with K elevation, calcium is given immediately while transcellular-shift treatment is prepared, but calcium must never be mistaken for potassium removal.
- For profound changes, 10 mL of 10% calcium chloride supplies a similar elemental-calcium dose to approximately 30 mL of 10% calcium gluconate; give by the route and rate specified in the applicable resuscitation pathway and use safe access.
- An alternative pathway for stable non-arrest patients may recommend smaller repeated calcium-gluconate doses, so do not interchange arrest and non-arrest protocols without checking them.

## 4.3 Hypokalaemia: prevent arrhythmia, paralysis and refractory electrolyte depletion

- K below 3.5 mmol/L is low and **below 2.5 mmol/L is generally severe**.
- Causes include gastrointestinal and renal losses, diuretic/mineralocorticoid action, insulin, catecholamines, alkalosis and poor intake.
- ECG may show T-wave flattening, ST depression, U waves and QT/QU prolongation; severe deficiency may cause muscle weakness, ileus, rhabdomyolysis and paralysis.
- Hypokalaemia potentiates digoxin toxicity and increases susceptibility to ventricular arrhythmias, particularly with concurrent hypomagnesaemia.

- Assess the expected speed of correction and underlying cause.
- Replace **oral KCl** when feasible in a stable patient, as chloride repletion also helps contraction alkalosis.
- In symptomatic severe deficiency, arrhythmia, inability to use the gut or ongoing substantial losses, give IV KCl through an appropriate controlled infusion with continuous ECG and repeat blood tests.
- A common peripheral rate is **≤10 mmol/h**; higher rates, e.g. **20 mmol/h**, often require central access, cardiac monitoring and local critical-care policy.
- Profound life-threatening hypokalaemic arrest may require more aggressive carefully controlled resuscitation according to local ALS protocols.
- Never give undiluted KCl as a routine IV push.
- **Correct magnesium concurrently** or renal potassium wasting and arrhythmia may persist despite repeated K administration.

The decision to postpone elective surgery is contextual: consider absolute K, ECG, muscle weakness, ongoing losses, underlying cardiac pathology, trend and procedure stress. Mild chronic stable K 3.2 without ECG changes differs from a rapidly falling K 3.2 in a patient on insulin and high-dose diuretics.

## 4.4 Magnesium: a gatekeeper of potassium and cardiac excitability

- Magnesium is necessary for ATP-dependent reactions, ion channel function, neuromuscular transmission and normal potassium retention.
- Hypomagnesaemia is common in critical illness due to poor intake, diarrhoea, alcohol use, loop/thiazide diuretics, proton-pump inhibitors, aminoglycosides, amphotericin and recovery from tubular injury.
- A value around **<0.7 mmol/L** is low in many laboratories; **0.40 mmol/L**, as in an ANZCA 2014.2 SAQ, is severe and may cause tremor, tetany, seizures, ventricular ectopy, **torsades de pointes**, hypocalcaemia (impaired PTH release/action), and refractory hypokalaemia.

- Treat the cause and replenish magnesium, adjusting for renal clearance.
- For haemodynamically stable mild deficiency, oral preparations may suffice but cause diarrhoea; for significant symptomatic deficiency, IV **magnesium sulfate** is appropriate.
- A common adult regimen for symptomatic severe depletion is **2 g MgSO₄ IV over 10–20 minutes**, followed by further replacement over hours; torsades with haemodynamic compromise calls for rapid **2 g IV** and standard arrhythmia/defibrillation management.
- Dose units matter: **2 g MgSO₄ is ≈8 mmol magnesium**, not 2 mmol.
- Monitor ECG, deep tendon reflexes, respiratory rate, renal function and serum magnesium, particularly with repeat doses.

- Hypermagnesaemia generally results from renal insufficiency plus magnesium-containing laxatives/antacids or therapeutic infusion.
- It causes loss of reflexes, bradycardia, hypotension, neuromuscular weakness and respiratory depression.
- Stop magnesium, give **IV calcium** for life-threatening toxicity as a physiological antagonist, support airway/circulation and use dialysis when severe with renal failure.
- Potentiation of non-depolarising neuromuscular blockers is relevant during anaesthesia.

## 4.5 Calcium: interpret ionised calcium when physiology is unstable

- Total calcium varies with albumin, but it is **ionised calcium (iCa)** that affects myocardial contraction, excitability, coagulation and neuromuscular function.
- Alkalosis increases albumin binding, reducing iCa even if total calcium is unchanged.
- Conversely acidaemia raises the ionised fraction.
- Therefore ICU, major transfusion, liver failure, pancreatitis and acid–base disorders warrant direct iCa measurement rather than relying solely on albumin-corrected total calcium.

- Hypocalcaemia presents with perioral tingling, carpopedal spasm, stridor, seizures, hypotension, impaired contraction and QT prolongation.
- Mechanisms include low PTH or hypomagnesaemia, vitamin D deficiency, CKD, pancreatitis, massive citrate exposure (blood products), sepsis and alkalosis.
- Correct magnesium and the cause.
- When symptomatic or haemodynamically significant, give IV calcium (e.g. **10 mL of 10% calcium gluconate** over 10 minutes, then reassess; more may be needed depending on measured iCa and clinical response).
- Calcium chloride gives approximately three times more elemental calcium per 10 mL than gluconate and is more irritating to tissues.
- Avoid mixing calcium and bicarbonate or phosphate in the same line because precipitation can occur.
- In massive transfusion, monitor and replace iCa according to the measured concentration and cardiovascular status.

- Hypercalcaemia causes polyuria, dehydration, nausea, constipation, weakness, shortened QT, confusion and, at very high levels, arrhythmia or coma.
- Causes are primary hyperparathyroidism, malignancy (PTHrP, bone lysis or vitamin D), medications and granulomatous disease.
- Investigate **corrected and/or ionised calcium, PTH, kidney function, phosphate, ECG and volume status**.
- Start isotonic fluid carefully if hypovolaemic, avoid nephrotoxins and immobilisation, and use antiresorptive therapy (bisphosphonate or denosumab according to kidney function and specialist advice) with calcitonin for rapid temporary effect in severe symptomatic cases.
- Severe cases in renal failure or refractory crisis may require dialysis with appropriate dialysate calcium.

**Calcium emergency thresholds and treatments:**

- Interpret the corrected total-calcium value cautiously when albumin and pH are abnormal, and obtain ionised calcium in unstable patients.
- Severe hypercalcaemia of malignancy is commonly defined as total calcium >3.5 mmol/L (14 mg/dL).
- Treat dehydration if present while watching for renal or heart failure; choose definitive antiresorptive therapy based on aetiology and renal status, recognising that bisphosphonates and denosumab act over days.
- For severe malignancy-related hypercalcaemia, the Endocrine Society suggests calcitonin plus an antiresorptive initially; calcitonin (often 4 international units/kg SC/IM every 12 hours in adult protocols) gives a faster, transient effect and should usually be limited to 48–72 hours because of tachyphylaxis.
- In symptomatic severe hypocalcaemia, secure ECG monitoring, directly measure ionised calcium and magnesium, give titrated IV calcium and address citrate load, hypomagnesaemia or hypoparathyroidism; repeated doses or infusion may be needed.
- Avoid giving calcium and phosphate through the same lumen without compatibility checks.

## 4.6 Phosphate and glucose complete the picture

- Phosphate is essential for ATP, diaphragmatic and myocardial performance and red-cell oxygen delivery.
- Hypophosphataemia occurs with refeeding, insulin therapy during DKA, respiratory alkalosis, renal losses, sepsis and alcoholism.
- Severe depletion (often <0.3–0.5 mmol/L, particularly when symptomatic) can cause respiratory failure, myocardial dysfunction, weakness, haemolysis and rhabdomyolysis.
- Replace enterally if mild/stable; IV sodium or potassium phosphate is used for severe symptomatic deficiency with attention to concurrent potassium and calcium, because rapid infusion can precipitate hypocalcaemia and calcium-phosphate deposition.
- Hyperphosphataemia occurs in AKI/CKD, rhabdomyolysis, tumour lysis and massive cell breakdown, often exacerbating hypocalcaemia.

- **Hypoglycaemia** may cause adrenergic symptoms (sweating, tremor, tachycardia) followed by neuroglycopenia (confusion, focal deficits, seizures, coma).
- Measure capillary/venous glucose immediately in any altered-consciousness patient.
- If conscious and safe to swallow, give rapidly absorbed oral glucose and recheck; if impaired consciousness, give IV dextrose—for example **10–25 g** with concentration/volume chosen to minimise extravasation—and repeat as necessary.
- IM glucagon is an alternative if IV access is unavailable, but response may be reduced in malnutrition, liver failure and depleted glycogen.
- Identify insulin/sulfonylurea error, alcohol, sepsis, liver/adrenal failure and delayed renal clearance; sulfonylurea-associated recurrent hypoglycaemia may require **octreotide** and observation.

- **Hyperglycaemia** worsens osmotic diuresis, immune function, endothelial injury and wound healing.
- In ICU and perioperative care, a pragmatic general target is approximately **6–10 mmol/L** (some critically ill settings tolerate up to 10–12 to avoid hypoglycaemia); avoid overly tight insulin targets because severe hypoglycaemia is harmful.
- A very high glucose does not by itself define DKA or HHS: measure **ketones, acid–base status and osmolality**.
- The distinction becomes crucial in Chapter 5.

**Glucose targets require clinical context:**

- The perioperative 6–10 mmol/L target quoted above is a commonly used operational range, not a universal ICU target or permission to drive every glucose toward 6. In critically ill adults, a conventional starting target is approximately 7.8–10 mmol/L (140–180 mg/dL), with individual adjustment for hypoglycaemia risk and local protocols.
- The NICE-SUGAR trial demonstrated harm with very tight ICU glucose control.
- Treat a patient with seizure, coma or neurological dysfunction from hypoglycaemia immediately with IV glucose rather than waiting for laboratory confirmation; after the initial response, look for recurrent hypoglycaemia, particularly with sulfonylurea exposure, long-acting insulin, kidney dysfunction or liver failure.

items.title: 5. Endocrine emergencies—DKA, HHS, adrenal crisis and thyroid storm
items.priority: P1 CORE (2 parent LOs) + P2 HIGH (1 parent LO)
items.body:
## 5.1 A shared principle: an endocrine emergency is a failure of feedback under stress

- Endocrine crises are dangerous because normal compensatory responses fail while surgery, infection, trauma or drug omission increases demand.
- Insulin deficiency prevents glucose utilisation and restraining of ketogenesis
- Cortisol deficiency impairs vascular response to catecholamines and may produce hypoglycaemia and hyponatraemia
- Excess thyroid hormone exaggerates metabolic demand and sympathetic responsiveness.
- These conditions can mimic each other or coexist with sepsis.
- Diagnosis and treatment therefore run concurrently: manage airway, perfusion, glucose, electrolytes, temperature and the trigger, while measuring hormone-specific tests.

## 5.2 Diabetic ketoacidosis: insulin deficiency creates both ketones and total-body electrolyte loss

- Normal insulin limits adipose lipolysis and hepatic ketogenesis, while facilitating peripheral glucose uptake.
- In DKA, absolute or relative insulin deficiency plus glucagon, catecholamines, cortisol and growth hormone drives lipolysis; hepatic ketones (especially **β-hydroxybutyrate**) accumulate as organic acids.
- Hyperglycaemia increases filtered glucose, causes osmotic diuresis and depletes water, sodium, potassium, magnesium and phosphate.
- Potassium may initially appear high because insulin deficiency, extracellular hypertonicity and acidemia shift K out of cells, while the body is actually **potassium-depleted**.
- Once insulin and volume are replaced, potassium can fall rapidly—one of the greatest dangers of DKA treatment.

- The [2024 international consensus](https://doi.org/10.2337/dci24-0032) diagnoses DKA using **all three** components: (D) known diabetes or plasma glucose **≥11.1 mmol/L**, (K) blood **β-hydroxybutyrate ≥3 mmol/L** or significant urine ketones if blood testing unavailable, and (A) **pH <7.30 and/or bicarbonate <18 mmol/L**.
- The lower glucose threshold and allowance for known diabetes avoid missing **euglycaemic DKA**, particularly associated with SGLT2 inhibitors, reduced caloric intake, pregnancy and postoperative stress.
- Do not rely on urinary nitroprusside ketones to follow resolution: it measures mostly acetoacetate, which may rise while β-hydroxybutyrate is being converted during recovery.

- Assess severity by acidemia, ketone concentration, cognition and organ failure.
- The consensus suggests severe DKA when β-hydroxybutyrate >6 mmol/L, pH <7.0 or bicarbonate <10, and/or stupor/coma
- Moderate DKA around pH 7.0–7.25 and bicarbonate 10–<15
- Milder DKA pH >7.25 to <7.30 or bicarbonate 15–18, while recognising that not every category feature must be present.
- Search actively for triggers: omitted insulin, infection, MI, pancreatitis, corticosteroids, SGLT2 drugs, pregnancy, pump malfunction or new-onset diabetes.

**Resuscitation begins with circulation and potassium measurement:**

- In adults without heart/kidney compromise, isotonic saline or a balanced crystalloid at around **500–1000 mL/h for the first 2–4 hours** is consistent with the consensus, titrated to perfusion, corrected sodium, urine output and fluid overload risk.
- The average deficit may be many litres, but it should not be replaced blindly.
- For frail, older, cardiac failure or ESKD patients use small reassessed boluses (e.g., **250 mL**) and evaluate whether fluid overload or dialysis dependence changes usual assumptions.
- Balanced solutions may reduce hyperchloraemic acidosis that can otherwise obscure recovery.

**Potassium determines when insulin is safe:**

- If K **<3.5 mmol/L**, replace potassium and **withhold insulin** until it rises >3.5 because insulin can precipitate fatal arrhythmia or respiratory muscle weakness.
- If potassium is 3.5–5.0 and renal output is sufficient, add KCl to fluids, commonly **20–30 mmol/L** aiming for serum K 4–5; if >5, withhold replacement initially and measure frequently.
- Do not give routine K in anuric end-stage kidney disease.
- Check glucose hourly or 1–2 hourly, and ketones/electrolytes/venous pH about every four hours initially (more frequently when unstable).
- Early K monitoring is needed after insulin commences.

- For substantial DKA, give IV short-acting insulin around **0.1 units/kg/h**, once potassium is safe.
- Insulin stops ketogenesis, the central target of treatment.
- When glucose decreases to around **13.9 mmol/L**, add **5–10% dextrose** and reduce IV insulin as per protocol (often to ≈0.05 units/kg/h) so **ketones continue clearing without hypoglycaemia**.
- A fall in glucose is not equivalent to resolution of DKA.
- Resolution in the 2024 consensus uses β-hydroxybutyrate **<0.6 mmol/L** plus venous pH ≥7.3 or bicarbonate ≥18; do not rely on urine ketones or anion gap alone, because saline-associated hyperchloraemia may persist after ketogenesis has ceased.
- For selected uncomplicated mild/moderate DKA, closely supervised subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin can be appropriate; not for severe haemodynamic instability or unconscious patients.

- Bicarbonate is **not routine** in DKA and has no demonstrated clinical benefit in most cases; it can worsen hypokalaemia, intracellular/CSF acidosis and potential cerebral complications.
- The 2024 consensus allows consideration when **pH <7.0**, guided by the full clinical picture.
- Phosphate should not be routinely replaced, but severe depletion **<1.0 mmol/L with muscle weakness or respiratory/cardiac dysfunction** may justify replacement.
- Manage infection/MI/pump failure and consider venous thromboembolism prevention as clinically indicated.

**Transfer from IV to subcutaneous insulin requires overlap:**

- Give basal insulin at least **1–2 hours before** stopping the infusion (some protocols 2–4 h), ensure the patient is eating or has a clear nutrition plan, and confirm sustained ketone resolution.
- Stopping IV insulin the instant glucose becomes normal causes rebound ketoacidosis.
- In SGLT2-associated euglycaemic DKA, glucose-containing fluids are often needed earlier while insulin continues, and the precipitating drug must be held.

**Perioperative relevance:**

- Non-urgent elective surgery should be postponed until DKA has resolved and its precipitant is addressed.
- Emergency surgery may be essential for source control; then treat DKA in parallel with arterial/venous gas and hourly glucose, maintain insulin–dextrose delivery, prevent dangerous potassium shifts and plan postoperative high-acuity monitoring.
- Intubation of a severely acidotic spontaneously hyperventilating patient can abruptly remove respiratory compensation (Chapter 2).

**Perioperative DKA and SGLT2-associated ketoacidosis:**

- Elective operations should not proceed in active DKA, even when serum glucose is only mildly increased.
- SGLT2 inhibitors can facilitate euglycaemic DKA with fasting, infection, low carbohydrate intake or reduced insulin; the 2026 ADA hospital guidance recommends stopping most SGLT2 inhibitors at least 3 days before elective surgery and ertugliflozin 4 days before.
- In unplanned surgery, ask directly about SGLT2 exposure and check beta-hydroxybutyrate, bicarbonate and anion gap if nausea, tachypnoea or unexplained acidosis develops despite glucose <11–14 mmol/L.
- Continue insulin with an adequate glucose substrate until ketogenesis resolves.
- For surgery that cannot wait because source control is lifesaving, insulin/glucose/electrolyte treatment, ventilation, haemodynamic resuscitation and postoperative ICU/HDU disposition must be planned together; the aim is safer physiology, not cancellation of necessary surgery.

## 5.3 Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state: profound dehydration with enough insulin to suppress major ketosis

- HHS develops over days to weeks, frequently in older patients with type 2 diabetes during infection, missed medication, stroke, MI or steroid exposure.
- Residual insulin restrains lipolysis and ketone production, but is insufficient to control hepatic glucose output or prevent osmotic diuresis.
- The result is extreme **water loss**, hypertonicity, neurological dysfunction and prerenal/structural kidney injury.
- Compared with DKA, the dominant immediate danger is often profound circulatory depletion and hyperosmolality rather than acidaemia.

- The 2024 consensus describes HHS by **glucose ≥33.3 mmol/L**, effective serum osmolality **>300 mOsm/kg** or total osmolality **>320 mOsm/kg**, **absence of significant ketonaemia** (β-hydroxybutyrate <3 mmol/L), and absence of marked acidosis (pH ≥7.3 and bicarbonate ≥15).
- Mixed DKA/HHS is common; if significant ketones and acidosis are present, manage the **DKA component**, not HHS as an isolated state.
- Effective osmolality (2Na + glucose) better reflects neuronal water shifts; total osmolality (2Na + glucose + urea) captures the often striking azotaemia and overall solute burden.

**Fluid first, controlled osmolality decline:**

- Restore effective circulation with carefully reassessed isotonic fluid; sodium may rise initially as glucose falls and water shifts intracellularly, without implying failure of rehydration.
- Monitor urine output, heart/lung signs, corrected sodium and osmolality.
- Aim for a decline in osmolality around **3–8 mOsm/kg/h** and glucose fall **≤5–6.7 mmol/L/h**; avoid a sodium fall >10 mmol/L in 24 hours.
- Rapid correction of chronic hypertonicity may cause cerebral oedema.
- When fluids alone reduce glucose and osmolality appropriately, insulin need not be aggressive early; start IV insulin commonly **0.05 units/kg/h** when indicated, after potassium and initial volume replacement.
- If mixed DKA/HHS exists, use a DKA insulin regimen (≈0.1 units/kg/h).
- Prevent hypoglycaemia and abrupt osmolality decline by adding dextrose as glucose approaches target while continuing necessary insulin.

**Complications and follow-up:**

- Thrombosis, AKI, rhabdomyolysis, electrolyte shifts, cerebral oedema and underlying sepsis/MI/stroke.
- Treat the precipitant, consider VTE prophylaxis unless contraindicated, and establish diabetes education and a sustainable discharge regimen.
- Unlike DKA, resolution includes improved consciousness and hydration, adequate urine output and effective/osmolar correction rather than simply disappearance of ketones.
- The [JBDS HHS pathway](https://abcd.care/sites/default/files/site_uploads/JBDS_Guidelines_Current/JBDS_06_HHS_care_pathway_in_adults_2022.pdf) provides a detailed rate-of-change algorithm.

**HHS correction is tracked by osmolality and clinical recovery:**

- The diagnosis of isolated HHS requires little significant ketosis and no major acidemia; substantial ketones or an anion-gap acidosis should trigger a mixed DKA/HHS pathway.
- Initial fluid replacement may lower glucose even before insulin starts.
- During therapy, track measured sodium, corrected sodium, osmolality and neurological status; as glucose falls, the measured sodium commonly rises without necessarily indicating a worsening free-water deficit.
- A precipitous decline in effective tonicity is more concerning than failure to normalise glucose rapidly.
- The 2024 international consensus considers HHS resolved when osmolality falls below approximately 300 mOsm/kg, glucose is below about 13.9 mmol/L, urine output is >0.5 mL/kg/h and mental status improves.
- Elderly patients with HF or CKD need repeated smaller reassessments rather than fixed large-volume prescriptions.

## 5.4 Adrenal crisis: loss of cortisol makes vasopressors and metabolic compensation fail

- Cortisol supports vascular α-adrenergic responsiveness, gluconeogenesis, appropriate free-water clearance and cardiovascular adaptation to stress.
- Primary adrenal failure also reduces aldosterone and causes salt wasting, hyperkalaemia and hypovolaemia.
- Secondary/tertiary failure caused by pituitary/hypothalamic disease or steroid suppression usually preserves aldosterone more effectively, so hyperkalaemia is less typical.
- A patient taking long-term glucocorticoids can have a suppressed hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis even if they appear well on usual maintenance doses.
- Infection, vomiting, trauma, childbirth and anaesthesia may suddenly exceed their ability to mount a stress cortisol response.

- Suspect adrenal crisis with **refractory hypotension**, hypovolaemia, abdominal pain, vomiting, fever, confusion, hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia and possibly hyperkalaemia.
- The phenotype is not specific; sepsis may coexist.
- Draw cortisol and ACTH before treatment **if this does not delay therapy**, with glucose, electrolytes, blood gas, cultures and tests for the trigger.
- A normal random cortisol in severe stress may still be inappropriately low; interpretation depends on timing, albumin, exogenous steroids and critical illness.

- The [Society for Endocrinology emergency guidance](https://www.endocrinology.org/clinical-practice/clinical-guidance/adrenal-crisis/) is deliberately simple: **hydrocortisone 100 mg IV/IM immediately**, then **200 mg over 24 h** by infusion or **50 mg IV every 6 h**, plus rapid IV isotonic crystalloid and glucose correction as appropriate.
- The first dose must never wait for assay results.
- Treat infection/bleeding/other stressors, monitor haemodynamics, sodium, K, glucose and fluid balance, and liaise with endocrinology for taper and maintenance glucocorticoid/mineralocorticoid replacement.
- In primary adrenal insufficiency, fludrocortisone becomes relevant once hydrocortisone has been reduced to replacement levels; high-dose hydrocortisone has sufficient mineralocorticoid activity during the initial crisis.

**Anaesthetic implications:**

- Establish whether a patient has known Addison disease, prior adrenalectomy, pituitary disease or potentially suppressive steroid exposure.
- For a patient in an active crisis, resuscitate and give hydrocortisone before non-essential anaesthesia; if emergency surgery is mandatory, continue resuscitation and perioperative stress dosing while securing haemodynamics.
- Ketamine/etomidate considerations need context: etomidate inhibits adrenal steroidogenesis and should be avoided when adrenal function is already critically impaired if alternatives are available.
- Give clear plans for postoperative steroids and sick-day education to prevent recurrence.

## 5.5 Thyroid storm: extreme hormonal activity plus organ dysfunction, not simply a high free T₄

- Thyroid hormone increases basal metabolic rate, thermogenesis, adrenergic sensitivity, cardiac rate and cardiac output.
- Thyroid storm is a **clinical** syndrome of severe thyrotoxicosis with multisystem decompensation, often triggered by infection, surgery, iodine load, labour, trauma or withdrawal of antithyroid drugs.
- Fever (sometimes >40°C), marked tachycardia/AF, agitation or delirium, vomiting/diarrhoea, jaundice, heart failure and shock are warning signs.
- Blood thyroid hormone concentrations alone do **not** distinguish storm reliably from uncomplicated thyrotoxicosis.
- Measure TSH, free T₄/T₃, glucose, renal/liver tests, electrolytes, ECG and search for triggers.
- The Burch–Wartofsky scale is supportive (≥45 strongly suggests storm; 25–44 suggests impending crisis) but treatment is not withheld pending a score.

- Treatment simultaneously targets **physiological collapse, thyroid-hormone synthesis, release and peripheral effects**.
- Admit to ICU/HDU when organ dysfunction is present.
- Provide oxygen, cautious fluid resuscitation, active cooling and **paracetamol rather than aspirin** (salicylates may increase circulating free thyroid hormones).
- Identify sepsis, MI and medication issues.
- Rate control with β-blockade decreases sympathetic effects and, at high doses, propranolol reduces T₄-to-T₃ conversion.
- **However, indiscriminate high-dose β-blockade may precipitate cardiovascular collapse** if tachycardia is compensating for low output or thyrotoxic cardiomyopathy.
- Use echocardiography; in unstable cardiac patients consider titratable short-acting **esmolol**, small doses and invasive monitoring.
- The [August 2026 multinational joint consensus](https://doi.org/10.1530/ETJ-26-0043) describes oral propranolol **60–80 mg every 4 h** for suitable stable patients, with IV esmolol often preferred where rapid withdrawal could be necessary.

- Thionamides inhibit synthesis: **propylthiouracil (PTU)** also inhibits peripheral T₄-to-T₃ conversion but carries important hepatic toxicity; **carbimazole/methimazole** is often preferred depending on context and route.
- Example commonly used storm regimens are PTU **500–1000 mg loading then 250 mg every 4–6 h**, or methimazole **20 mg every 4–6 h**, specialist-selected.
- In liver injury, PTU risk is particularly relevant.
- **Give iodide at least one hour after the thionamide** to block thyroid hormone release via the acute Wolff–Chaikoff effect; giving iodine first risks providing substrate for new hormone production in synthesis-driven disease.
- The 2026 statement describes Lugol solution **8 drops four times daily** or saturated potassium iodide **5 drops four times daily**, with local preparation strength and dilution verified.
- Iodide is less useful in destructive thyroiditis, where hormone release is not primarily de novo synthesis.

- Give glucocorticoids—e.g., **hydrocortisone 100 mg IV then 50 mg every 6 h**—to reduce conversion and cover relative adrenal insufficiency.
- Consider **cholestyramine** as an adjunct to interrupt enterohepatic hormone cycling.
- If refractory, discuss therapeutic plasma exchange and **urgent thyroidectomy**, occasionally supported by mechanical circulatory support when cardiogenic shock is profound.
- Once clinically stabilised, plan definitive endocrine therapy.
- TSH lags behind improvement and is not an early treatment endpoint; follow heart rate, fever, consciousness, circulatory support and free hormones.

- **The exam-relevant perioperative scenario** is urgent thyroidectomy after failed medical control (2023.2 SAQ), or intraoperative/post-thyroidectomy crisis (2012.1 and earlier SAQs).
- Optimise all feasible components, treat arrhythmias and high output failure, consider a controlled airway given goitre/tracheal factors, prepare arterial monitoring and short-acting haemodynamic agents, avoid abrupt catecholamine surges and anticipate postoperative airway compromise, hypocalcaemia and continued high-risk storm physiology.
- A carefully prepared operation under specialist multidisciplinary support may be safer than prolonged uncontrolled storm when maximal medical therapy has failed.

**Before thyroid surgery and after recovery:**

- If urgent thyroidectomy is indicated despite inadequate medical control, the objective is to reduce adrenergic and metabolic instability as far as the available time permits, not to demand a normal TSH (which can remain suppressed).
- Evaluate atrial fibrillation, ischemia, high-output or low-output heart failure with focused echocardiography, and airway distortion or compression from goitre.
- Arrange ICU-level perioperative observation, arterial monitoring when warranted, rapid access to short-acting rate control and vasopressors, and continuation of antithyroid treatment until definitive control.
- Hypotension after beta-blockade in storm may reflect previously masked cardiomyopathy; reflex escalation of beta-blocker can be dangerous.
- Post-thyroidectomy monitoring includes persistent storm physiology, haematoma/airway obstruction, hypocalcaemia, recurrent laryngeal nerve injury and later hypothyroid replacement.
- These specific decisions are relevant to the 2023.2 ANZCA SAQ on urgent thyroidectomy after failed medical treatment.

items.title: 6. Acute kidney injury: physiology, diagnosis and prevention
items.priority: P1 CORE (1 parent LO) + P3 MODERATE (2 parent LOs) + P5 MINIMUM (2 parent LOs)
items.body:
## 6.1 Think of the kidney as a flow-, pressure- and oxygen-sensitive regulator

- Renal blood flow is exceptionally high relative to kidney mass, but oxygen tension in the medulla is comparatively low because countercurrent exchange and active sodium transport create an inherent supply–demand tension.
- The kidney autoregulates GFR across a range of perfusion pressures through myogenic responses and tubuloglomerular feedback.
