KDIGO defines it as a creatinine rise of 26 µmol/L within 48 hours, a rise to 1.5 times baseline within 7 days, or urine output below 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 hours. Prevention rests on identifying risk, maintaining mean arterial pressure and euvolaemia (goal-directed therapy has some support), avoiding nephrotoxins and contrast, and treating sepsis. The acidosis review adds that accumulation of phosphate, sulphate and urate anions causes a high anion gap acidosis in renal failure; acidaemia then drives hyperkalaemia.

> **Examiner's point:** much of the mark allocation was for factors, so spend time on part (a); RIFLE criteria, nephrotoxins, surgical, patient, anaesthetic and postoperative factors.

## Audit clarification and extension

Use complete KDIGO 2012 functional staging rather than the shorthand “stages 1–3” alone: stage 1 creatinine 1.5–1.9 times baseline or ≥26.5 micromol/L rise, UO <0.5 mL/kg/h for 6–12 h; stage 2 creatinine 2.0–2.9 times or UO <0.5 for ≥12 h; stage 3 creatinine ≥3 times, ≥353.6 micromol/L with acute change, or KRT, or UO <0.3 for ≥24 h/anuria ≥12 h. Confirm baseline and time course. The KDIGO 2026 AKI/AKD document located during this audit is a public-review draft, not a final guideline to cite as settled policy. New evidence is discussed in the dedicated prevention model: risk-targeted bundles, biomarkers and post-AKI follow-up are more defensible than a blanket “nothing works”. Sources: official report; KDIGO; BigpAK-2 and current BJAEd cardiac AKI review.

items.title: 2010.2 Q13: Outline the principles of an initial management plan for diabetic keto
items.q: Outline the principles of an initial management plan for diabetic ketoacidosis, having regard to the physiological derangements involved.
items.model:
## Approach: plan paired with physiology

| Step | Management | Physiological reason |
|---|---|---|
| **1. Resuscitate** | ABC; oxygen; monitoring; IV access; send glucose, ketones, gas, electrolytes, urea, creatinine, FBC, cultures, ECG | Hypovolaemia, acidosis and arrhythmia risk |
| **2. Fluids** | **0.9% saline (or balanced crystalloid) 10 mL/kg/h initially** (1 L over the first hour in an adult, then reassess); total deficit about 100 mL/kg over 24–48 hours | **Osmotic diuresis** causes loss of water (about 6 L) and sodium, chloride and potassium; fluid restores perfusion and reduces counter-regulatory hormones |
| **3. Potassium** | Add **KCl 20–40 mmol/L** once K falls below about 5.0 under current adult consensus and urine output is present; if K below 3.5, give potassium before insulin; monitor hourly | **Total body potassium deficit** despite normal or high serum K (acidosis and insulin deficiency shift K out of cells); insulin and correction of acidosis shift K into cells and risk **hypokalaemia** |
| **4. Insulin** | **Fixed-rate IV insulin 0.1 units/kg/h** after fluids started (and K above 3.5); no bolus in many protocols | Inhibits lipolysis and ketogenesis, and clears ketones; the aim is to **stop ketone production**, not rapidly normalise glucose; fall in glucose about 3–5 mmol/L/h |
| **5. Glucose** | Add **10% dextrose** when glucose falls below 14 mmol/L (continue insulin) | Allows insulin to clear ketones without hypoglycaemia |
| **6. Treat the cause** | Infection, ischaemia, missed insulin, pancreatitis, drugs (SGLT2 inhibitors) | Precipitant |
| **7. Acidosis** | **Bicarbonate is not recommended** unless pH below 7.0 under current adult consensus (limited evidence; risks hypokalaemia, paradoxical CNS acidosis) | Acidosis resolves with fluids and insulin |
| **8. Monitoring** | Glucose and ketones hourly, gas and electrolytes 2–4 hourly (with **magnesium** and phosphate), urine output, GCS | Detect hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, hypoglycaemia, cerebral oedema |
| **9. Ventilation** | Supportive ventilation if unable to compensate (exhaustion, reduced GCS), matching minute ventilation | Respiratory compensation fails |

## Further points

Resolution criteria: ketones below 0.6 mmol/L and pH above 7.3 (not glucose alone); transition to subcutaneous insulin with overlap of at least 1–2 hours under the current basal-bolus/IV insulin protocol; watch for **cerebral oedema** (especially in children and young adults), pulmonary oedema, and venous thromboembolism.

## Evidence

The acidosis review's worked DKA case (pH 6.9, bicarbonate 4, lactate 7, creatinine 308) was left, after 6 litres of 0.9% saline and insulin, with a normal gap but persisting acidosis from chloride excess, a reason to prefer balanced crystalloid once volume is restored. pH below 6.9 in DKA does not carry the mortality of lactic acidosis, and DKA is primarily managed with insulin, fluid and electrolytes. Bicarbonate is not routine, with selected consideration for pH <7.0 in current adult consensus. Blue Book 2019 adds that in SGLT2 inhibitor users DKA can occur with glucose below 14 mmol/L and needs more dextrose.

> **Examiner's point:** the best answers set out the plan in sequence and linked each step to its pathophysiology, and mentioned magnesium and the lack of evidence for bicarbonate.

## Audit clarification and extension

Current adult DKA diagnosis requires diabetes/hyperglycaemia (glucose ≥11.1 mmol/L or known diabetes), significant ketonaemia (beta-hydroxybutyrate ≥3 mmol/L) and metabolic acidosis (pH <7.3 and/or HCO3 <18). Euglycaemic presentations are possible, especially with SGLT2 inhibitors. Start isotonic saline or balanced crystalloid at an individual rate (500–1000 mL/h for the first 2–4 h in suitable adults, smaller boluses in frail/cardiac/renal patients), then reassess. If K <3.5, replace and delay insulin until corrected; add maintenance replacement when K falls below about 5, targeting 4–5. When glucose <13.9 add 5–10% dextrose and usually reduce IV insulin to about 0.05 units/kg/h while clearing ketosis. Do not stop insulin for normal glucose alone. Resolution is ketones <0.6 and pH ≥7.3 or HCO3 ≥18; a saline-related NAGMA can make anion gap/bicarbonate alone misleading. Bicarbonate is not routine; current consensus considers it only for severe acidosis, e.g. pH <7.0. These are adult principles; children need their own protocol. Source: official 2010.2 feedback; ADA/EASD/JBDS/AACE/DTS consensus 2024.
rubric: Insulin to stop ketogenesis, not normalise glucose

items.title: 2009.2 Q4: A 70 year old female had a cardiac arrest after arriving in the Recove
items.q: A 70 year old female had a cardiac arrest after arriving in the Recovery Room following open fixation of a femoral fracture. This arterial blood gas was taken after intubation and several minutes of CPR. FiO2 1.0; pH 6.93; PaO2 160 mmHg; PaCO2 78 mmHg; HCO3 16 mmol/L; base excess -14 mmol/L; lactate 11 mmol/L; K 5.8 mmol/L. [Values supplied for study purposes: the original report does not print the gas, so these are illustrative values consistent with the examiners' description of a severe mixed respiratory and metabolic acidosis.] Interpret this gas. Explain what additional information you need. Describe the likely causes.
items.model:
## Interpretation

- **Severe acidaemia**: pH 6.93 ([H+] about 117 nmol/L; check 24 × 78 / 16 ≈ 117).
- **Respiratory acidosis**: PaCO2 78 is markedly raised.
- **Metabolic acidosis**: HCO3 16, base excess -14, **lactate 11**. If it were an acute respiratory acidosis alone, HCO3 would be about 27–28, so the low value shows a metabolic component. Winter's formula predicts a PaCO2 of about 32 ± 2 for a metabolic acidosis with HCO3 16; the measured 78 shows the lack of respiratory compensation.
- **Mixed severe respiratory and metabolic (lactic) acidosis**; neither disorder compensates for the other.
- **Oxygenation**: PAO2 on FiO2 1.0 ≈ 713 − 78/0.8 ≈ 615 mmHg; PaO2 160 gives an **A–a gradient of about 450 mmHg and a PaO2/FiO2 of 160**: a large shunt or V/Q problem (poor pulmonary flow during CPR, aspiration, embolism, pulmonary oedema, atelectasis, or tube position).
- **Potassium 5.8**: acidosis and tissue hypoperfusion.

## Explanation (must explain both components)

- **Metabolic (lactic) acidosis**: absent or inadequate circulation causes **peripheral hypoperfusion and anaerobic metabolism**; the delay or inadequacy of external cardiac compression allowed lactate to accumulate.
- **Respiratory acidosis**: **absent or inadequate ventilation** (no brainstem perfusion, so no respiratory drive); ventilation after intubation has been **inadequate or too brief to clear the accumulated CO2**, and CO2 clearance depends on pulmonary blood flow, which is low during CPR.

## Additional information needed

Timeline of the arrest and the duration and quality of CPR, minute ventilation and tube position (ETCO2), the cardiac rhythm, haemoglobin, ionised calcium, glucose, **blood loss and haemodynamics before arrest**, drugs given (opioids, bicarbonate, adrenaline), and previous gas results.

## Likely causes of the arrest in this patient

**Pulmonary embolism (thrombus or fat) after femoral fracture fixation**, **fat embolism or bone cement implantation syndrome**, **haemorrhage/ hypovolaemia**, myocardial ischaemia, **residual anaesthetic or opioid effect with hypoventilation and hypoxia**, anaphylaxis (antibiotic or cement), hyperkalaemia, and tension pneumothorax. Any aetiology must account for **both** the respiratory and the metabolic components (dual pathology is acceptable).

## Management

Continue ALS with good-quality CPR and adrenaline, ensure effective ventilation (10 breaths/minute once intubated, titrated to ETCO2), treat reversible causes, consider bicarbonate only for severe acidosis with hyperkalaemia, and provide post-resuscitation ICU care.

## Evidence

The acidosis review reports that lactic acidosis with pH below 6.9 reduces myocardial contractility and strongly predicts death, and that lactate in trauma, septic or cardiogenic shock has the worst outcome. BICAR-ICU was neutral for its primary composite from bicarbonate; the retrospective paediatric cohort found no mortality association with benefit, with more hypocalcaemia, hypokalaemia and hypernatraemia. Restore ventilation first, since bicarbonate generates carbon dioxide.

> **Examiner's point:** most candidates scored on interpretation but failed the later parts; the cause must explain both the respiratory and metabolic components, with an organised answer.

## Audit clarification and extension

The original report page was visually checked: it does not display the numeric gas. The values retained in this study stem are **illustrative, not an authenticated historical exam table**; calculations apply to that example only. Do not attribute its exact PaO2, potassium or lactate to ANZCA. During CPR use the ALS ventilation rate and capnography to assess tube position/CPR, but do not hyperventilate solely to normalise ETCO2 (low flow lowers ETCO2). Routine bicarbonate is not indicated for arrest-associated lactic acidosis; use a specific hyperkalaemic/toxicological indication where appropriate. The actual examiner point is explanation of both metabolic and respiratory components. Source: official 2009.2 report and current ALS principles.
rubric: Recognises severe mixed respiratory and metabolic acidosis
Uses compensation rules to show a mixed disorder
Interprets oxygenation with FiO2 and A–a gradient
Additional information requested (timeline, ETCO2, ionised calcium)
Perioperative causes of arrest (embolism, haemorrhage) and management

items.title: 2008.1 Q6: The electrolyte results below were taken from a 38 year old woman foun
items.q: The electrolyte results below were taken from a 38 year old woman found obtunded 30 hours after abdominal hysterectomy. She had no intercurrent illnesses prior to surgery. Explain how these electrolyte abnormalities are most likely to have arisen and describe how you would correct them. Sodium 110 (135-145); potassium 3 (3.0-5.0); chloride 80 (95-105); bicarbonate 25 (20-32); glucose 5.0 (3.0-5.5); urea 3.0 (3.0-8.0); creatinine 0.06 (0.06-0.12); measured osmolality 225 mosmol/kg (280-295).
items.model:
## Interpretation

**Severe, acute hypotonic hyponatraemia** (sodium 110, measured osmolality 225; true hypotonicity, not pseudo- or hyperglycaemic hyponatraemia, as glucose is 5 and the calculated osmolality of about 235 matches the measured value). The chloride is proportionately low, and potassium is borderline. The patient is **obtunded**, so she is **symptomatic with cerebral oedema** and at risk of seizures, respiratory arrest and brainstem herniation. This is a **critical emergency**; premenopausal women are at the highest risk of fatal cerebral oedema.

## How it arose (6 marks)

**Excess free water relative to sodium** in the first 30 hours:
- **Hypotonic IV fluids** (5% dextrose or 0.18% saline/ 4% dextrose) given postoperatively, plus oral water;
- **non-osmotic ADH release** (SIADH-like) from **surgical stress, pain, nausea, opioids, anaesthetic drugs** and hypovolaemia, impairing water excretion;
- additional factors: **thiazides, oxytocin or carbetocin** only if actually administered (not routine assumptions for an abdominal hysterectomy), gynaecological glycine or sorbitol irrigation absorption (not for abdominal approach), **vomiting with water replacement**, and adrenal insufficiency or hypothyroidism.

**Assessment to discriminate causes**: volume status (hypovolaemic, euvolaemic or hypervolaemic), fluid chart, drug chart, **urine sodium and osmolality** (above 100 mosmol/kg and sodium above 30 mmol/L suggests ADH-driven/ SIADH or diuretics), plasma osmolality, glucose, urea, uric acid, cortisol, TSH, chest X-ray, and CT head if focal signs.

## Correction (4 marks)

- **Emergency, ICU/HDU**: airway protection (intubation if GCS is low), oxygen, monitoring, seizure control.
- **Hypertonic saline (3%)**: **100–150 mL (or 2 mL/kg) bolus over 10 minutes**, repeated up to 2 more times until symptoms improve, aiming for a **rise of 4–6 mmol/L in the first 6 hours** (enough to reverse cerebral oedema) and a conservative **ceiling of 8 mmol/L in any 24 hours**, with a lower planned rise of 4–6 in patients at high ODS risk and specialist adjustment to the documented onset (avoid **osmotic demyelination**).
- **Sodium every 1–2 hours**; stop 3% saline once symptoms improve or the target is reached; if overcorrecting, give **desmopressin with 5% dextrose** to re-lower.
- **Stop hypotonic fluids**, then fluid restriction or isotonic saline according to volume status and urine studies; potassium replacement (also raises sodium); treat the cause.
- Avoid simple "admission for slow correction", which is inadequate.

## Evidence

BJA Education 2017 classes hyponatraemia as mild (130-135), moderate (125-129) or severe (125 or less); acute (under 48 hours) causes cerebral oedema. Initial tests: paired serum and urine osmolality, urinary sodium, glucose, thyroid function and cortisol. It limits correction to 4 to 6 mmol/L per 24 hours (12-14 in 48, 14-16 in 72), with sampling every 1 to 2 hours, 3% saline only for seizures or coma, and dextrose if sodium rises too fast. The 2022 neurosurgical review allows 10 mmol/L per 24 hours but notes demyelination risk with malnutrition, malignancy and liver failure.

> **Examiner's point:** formulate a differential, discriminate between causes with volume status and urine sodium and osmolality, recognise that obtunded means symptomatic, and discuss strong saline.

## Audit clarification and extension

Treat the severe neurological symptoms immediately with a protocolised 3% saline bolus (commonly 100 mL over 10 min or 150 mL over 20 min, reassess/repeat), aiming for an initial 4–6-mmol/L rise rather than normal sodium. Monitor urine output and sodium closely: spontaneous water diuresis after reversing ADH stimulation is a major overcorrection mechanism. Potassium replacement also increases effective sodium correction. If correction is running too fast, stop the corrective therapy and seek specialist-directed desmopressin plus electrolyte-free water/re-lowering. Do not diagnose SIADH without excluding adrenal failure, volume depletion and relevant drugs. Some duration is inferred from postoperative timing, but unknown baseline or high-risk features demand conservative later correction. Source: official 2008.1 report; current hyponatraemia treatment standard 2024 and sodium review.
rubric: Assessment (volume status, urine sodium and osmolality)
Correction limits to prevent osmotic demyelination
Stops hypotonic fluids and monitors sodium frequently

items.title: 2025.1 Q10: 2025.1 Q10 — Polyuria during craniotomy and arginine vasopressin defic
items.q: 2025.1 Q10 — Polyuria during craniotomy and arginine vasopressin deficiency
items.model:
**Official question:** List the potential causes of polyuria in a patient undergoing a craniotomy. (30%) Describe the diagnosis and management of intraoperative arginine vasopressin deficiency (formerly known as central diabetes insipidus). (70%)

## Causes — 30%

First verify the measured urine output and time course. Consider osmotic diuresis from mannitol, hyperglycaemia/glycosuria or a large solute load; loop diuretics; excess administered fluid; AVP deficiency after hypothalamic–pituitary damage; impaired renal response to AVP from lithium, hypercalcaemia or hypokalaemia; and recovery from AKI or relief of obstruction. Cold diuresis and mobilisation of previously retained fluid are further possibilities. Polyuria alone does not diagnose AVP deficiency.

## Diagnosis

Review lesion location, surgical manipulation, previous pituitary disease, drugs, fluids, glucose and baseline sodium. Confirm sustained unexpectedly high output, for example >2 mL/kg/h or >250–300 mL/h in an adult over several hours, interpreted against body size and administered fluid. Obtain contemporaneous serum sodium/osmolality, glucose, renal function and urine osmolality/specific gravity. The characteristic finding is **inappropriately dilute urine despite rising serum sodium or hyperosmolality**: urine osmolality often <300 mOsm/kg, specific gravity <1.005 and plasma osmolality >295–300. Thresholds support the pattern, not a stand-alone intraoperative diagnosis. Sodium may initially remain normal if losses are replaced. Glycosuria with a high urine osmolality supports osmotic diuresis instead. Formal water deprivation is unsafe during anaesthesia or unstable hypernatraemia; specialist testing can follow later if uncertainty persists.

## Management

Notify surgeon, senior anaesthetist, endocrine and ICU teams; monitor arterial pressure, perfusion, hourly urine, cumulative balance and repeated sodium/osmolality, glucose and potassium. Correct intravascular depletion with titrated isotonic crystalloid before prescribing free-water correction. Then replace appropriate maintenance, estimated deficit and ongoing losses using enteral water when safe or IV glucose 5%, adjusting to sodium trajectory. Do not continue blind litre-for-litre replacement once antidiuresis starts.

For convincing AVP deficiency with excessive dilute urine, an example adult rescue dose is desmopressin 1–2 micrograms IV/IM, under endocrine/local protocol; a titratable vasopressin infusion is an alternative in selected monitored operative/ICU settings. Routes are not dose-equivalent. Re-dose according to recurrent dilute polyuria and sodium trend, not an automatic frequent schedule. Established chronic treatment should not be inadvertently omitted.

During active resuscitation measure sodium about every 2–4 h or more often if rapidly changing. For chronic/uncertain hypernatraemia use controlled correction, commonly no more than 10 mmol/L/day, with individual specialist adjustment. Avoid overshoot and fluid overload after DDAVP. Anticipate postoperative transient AVP deficiency followed by SIADH and sometimes recurrent deficiency; arrange HDU/ICU handover and reassessment. Cortisol deficiency can mask AVP deficiency, which may appear after hydrocortisone. Document a specific postoperative fluid, sodium and DDAVP plan.

**Sources and review basis:** Actual 2025.1 examiner feedback reviewed; current endocrine AVP-deficiency guidance; BJAEd sodium review identified as supporting background. The three sections and 30/70 emphasis follow the paper; the /10 schedule is educator-created.
rubric: Causes: at least three mechanistically distinct possibilities (3 marks).
Diagnosis: sustained output, paired serum/urine pattern, glucose/solute differential and sodium may initially be normal (3).
Management: volume assessment; type/rate of replacement; DDAVP/AVP; sodium/output reassessment and postoperative hazards (4).

items.title: 2023.2 Q13: 2023.2 Q13 — Urgent thyroidectomy after failed medical treatment of th
items.q: 2023.2 Q13 — Urgent thyroidectomy after failed medical treatment of thyrotoxicosis
items.model:
**Official question:** Discuss the perioperative management of a patient undergoing urgent thyroidectomy following failed medical therapy for thyrotoxicosis.

## Assessment and preparation

Clarify why treatment failed: non-adherence, adverse effects, inadequate time, refractory hormone synthesis or a different mechanism such as thyroiditis. Thyrotoxicosis means excessive circulating hormone action; hyperthyroidism specifically means excess gland synthesis. Establish surgical urgency with endocrine, surgical, anaesthetic and ICU teams. Aim for clinical and biochemical control where time permits, but do not defer life-saving surgery for a normal TSH, which may lag recovery. Explain increased cardiovascular, airway and storm risks.

Assess temperature, cognition, hydration, tachyarrhythmia, heart failure, ischaemia and exercise tolerance. Review TFT trend, ECG, electrolytes/glucose, renal function, FBC and liver tests; echocardiography if cardiac dysfunction is suspected. Ask about beta blockers and antithyroid treatment, agranulocytosis/hepatotoxicity, previous surgery/radiotherapy, compression, stridor, dysphagia, positional dyspnoea and voice change. Review imaging for tracheal compression/retrosternal extension and vocal-cord assessment where indicated.

Continue appropriate antithyroid medication and beta blockade unless a specific contraindication exists. Failed medical therapy does not mean all drugs should be stopped. Endocrine-directed rapid preparation may combine thionamide, iodine after synthesis blockade, glucocorticoid and sometimes cholestyramine; refractory cases may require plasma exchange. Titrate beta blockade cautiously: a patient dependent on adrenergic support in low-output thyrotoxic cardiomyopathy may collapse after an indiscriminate bolus. Treat infection, dehydration, electrolyte disturbance and heart failure.

## Intraoperative care

Plan airway management from the actual examination and imaging, including an awake technique when indicated by obstruction or difficult rescue. Have difficult-airway and surgical rescue resources. Standard monitoring plus temperature, appropriate arterial pressure monitoring and reliable IV access; assess need for cardiac-output monitoring individually. Avoid large sympathetic responses to induction, intubation, incision and emergence; ensure adequate anaesthesia, analgesia and controlled ventilation. Choose drugs to minimise tachycardia, while maintaining coronary and systemic perfusion. Use neuromuscular monitoring and communicate if nerve monitoring changes relaxant requirements.

Watch for disproportionate tachycardia, hyperthermia, dysrhythmia, haemodynamic instability and increasing metabolic demand suggesting storm. Consider inadequate anaesthesia, sepsis, malignant hyperthermia and drug reactions. Seek help immediately and provide cooling, oxygenation, circulation support, endocrine-directed thionamide/iodine/steroid treatment and carefully selected rate control. Alpha blockade is not routine thyroid-storm preparation; do not confuse this disease with phaeochromocytoma.

## Emergence and postoperative care

Plan awake extubation after demonstrable recovery and airway assessment; deep extubation is not a default strategy for a potentially compromised thyroid airway. Consider postoperative ventilation when airway oedema, compression, bilateral recurrent-laryngeal injury, tracheomalacia or instability makes extubation unsafe. Monitor for neck haematoma/airway obstruction, hypocalcaemia, recurrent-laryngeal injury, pain, bleeding and recurrent storm. Use HDU/ICU when unstable/high risk. Agree antithyroid cessation, hormone replacement and calcium monitoring with endocrine/surgical teams.

**Sources and review basis:** Actual 2023.2 feedback reviewed. ATA thyroid-storm treatment guidance and 2026 joint consensus targeted recommendations; BJAEd thyroid/parathyroid article 2024 targeted thyroid and calcium sections reviewed after access was restored; crisis doses remain checked against primary endocrine guidance.

**Signed-in sweep verification:** the relevant thyroid-preparation sections of BJAEd 2024 were reviewed. The model retains primary-guidance crisis doses and an individualised extubation plan; elective preparation tables and apparent displayed unit issues are not universal emergency prescriptions.
rubric: Preassessment/urgency, cardiac state, investigations and compression/airway planning (3).
Medication continuation and rapid optimisation, including cautious beta blockade (2).
Intraoperative sympathetic control, monitoring and recognition/treatment of storm (3).
Extubation, haematoma/nerve/calcium surveillance and postoperative destination (2).

items.title: 2012.1 Q8: 2012.1 Q8 — Thyroid tests, timing of thyroidectomy and intraoperative
items.q: 2012.1 Q8 — Thyroid tests, timing of thyroidectomy and intraoperative storm
items.model:
**Official case:** A 35-year-old female is booked for thyroidectomy. TSH 0.1 (N 0.3–3 mIU/L), total T4 20 (N 4–11 micrograms/dL), free T4 4 (N 0.7–1.8 ng/dL), and free T3 120 (N 60–175 ng/dL), **as printed in the report**. Interpret the tests (10%); justify when to proceed (50%); manage intraoperative thyrotoxic crisis (40%). The T3 label/reference/unit combination is unusual; verify the actual laboratory assay rather than silently correcting the historical table.

## Interpretation — 10%

Suppressed TSH with elevated total and free T4 is overt biochemical thyrotoxicosis, with pituitary suppression by negative feedback. The printed T3 lies within its supplied interval; this does not negate the high free T4. Establish cause, symptoms, treatment and assay/drug interference where discordance exists.

## When to operate — 50%

Elective thyroidectomy should generally wait for adequate clinical control and preferably euthyroid circulating hormone concentrations to reduce storm, arrhythmia and cardiac-failure risk. A normal TSH is not an obligatory immediate endpoint because recovery can lag. Review symptom severity, heart rate/rhythm, blood pressure, temperature, volume status and cardiac function; ECG, TFT trend, FBC, electrolytes and relevant imaging support the decision. Identify compressive airway symptoms and vocal-cord dysfunction. Discuss urgency and achievable optimisation with endocrine and surgeon, including informed consent.

Thionamides inhibit new synthesis but do not immediately remove stored hormone, so preparation usually takes weeks. Continue therapy; control adrenergic symptoms with a carefully titrated beta blocker, considering cardiac function. Specialist-directed iodine after thionamide can rapidly reduce release and gland vascularity; steroid reduces peripheral conversion and provides stress cover in severe disease. Treat infection, dehydration and heart failure.

An airway emergency, progressive compression, or urgent refractory/life-threatening disease can outweigh the benefit of waiting. Stabilise as far as feasible, arrange an appropriate airway plan, experienced staff, invasive monitoring where justified, and postoperative ICU. Do not answer “never operate until normal TFTs”: this misses the examiner's emergency exception. Conversely, beta blockade alone does not make uncontrolled thyrotoxicosis harmless.

## Intraoperative crisis — 40%

Recognise a clinical syndrome of otherwise unexplained marked tachycardia/AF, hyperthermia, haemodynamic instability or failure, and CNS/GI manifestations when assessable. Do not wait for a hormone result to diagnose storm. Call for help, discuss stopping/postponing non-essential surgery, exclude hypoxia/hypercarbia and consider sepsis, malignant hyperthermia or inadequate anaesthesia. Provide oxygen, appropriate ventilation, cooling, titrated fluid and haemodynamic support; treat the precipitant and monitor glucose/electrolytes.

With endocrine/ICU help, use a high-dose thionamide for synthesis-driven disease: examples are PTU 500–1000 mg enteral loading then 250 mg every 4 h, or methimazole 60–80 mg/day. Give iodine at least one hour after thionamide using a pharmacy-verified formulation. These are crisis regimens, not ordinary maintenance doses. Give hydrocortisone, for example 100 mg IV every 8 h after an appropriate initial dose under protocol. Cautious short-acting beta blockade may control rate in an adequately perfused patient; avoid reflex large doses in low-output failure. Consider specialist rescue therapy, plasma exchange or mechanical circulatory support if refractory. Arrange ICU, serial response assessment and a definitive endocrine plan.

**Sources and review basis:** Actual 2012.1 report reviewed; ATA drug/dose table and current thyroid-storm consensus targeted recommendations. /10 emphasis follows the official 10/50/40 weighting, but is not its marking grid.

**Signed-in sweep verification:** the relevant thyroid-preparation sections of BJAEd 2024 were reviewed. The model retains primary-guidance crisis doses and an individualised extubation plan; elective preparation tables and apparent displayed unit issues are not universal emergency prescriptions.
rubric: Interpretation including elevated free T4 and suppressed TSH (1).
Timing: elective control, realistic drug time course, individual urgency/airway exception, multidisciplinary preparation (5).
Crisis recognition/differential, supportive care, thionamide→iodine, steroid and safe beta-blocker selection (4).

items.title: 2021.2 Q8: 2021.2 Q8 — Addison’s disease and urgent laparotomy for bowel obstruct
items.q: 2021.2 Q8 — Addison’s disease and urgent laparotomy for bowel obstruction
items.model:
**Official question:** Discuss how a diagnosis of Addison’s disease would influence your perioperative management of a patient who requires an urgent laparotomy for bowel obstruction.

## Implications and immediate priorities

Addison's disease is **primary adrenal insufficiency**, with deficient cortisol and usually aldosterone. Surgical stress increases cortisol requirements; bowel obstruction, vomiting and fasting make usual oral hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone unreliable. Cortisol deficiency reduces vascular responsiveness and gluconeogenesis, causing hypotension and hypoglycaemia; aldosterone deficiency causes sodium loss, volume depletion and hyperkalaemia. Distinguish this from central adrenal insufficiency, where aldosterone is usually preserved. Both hypovolaemia from obstruction and sepsis can coexist with an adrenal crisis.

Assess shock, mental state, glucose, sodium, potassium, renal function and acid–base status urgently; ECG for significant hyperkalaemia. Review previous crises, usual steroid doses, last retained dose, sick-day escalation, endocrine letters, emergency injection kit and associated autoimmune disease. Contact the patient's endocrine team or on-call endocrinologist. Samples for cortisol/ACTH may help an uncertain diagnosis if immediately available, but must not delay treatment in established disease or suspected crisis.

## Resuscitation and steroid replacement

Give **hydrocortisone 100 mg IV promptly**, including at induction for major surgery; then **200 mg over 24 h by infusion or 50 mg IV every 6 h** while critically ill/nil by mouth. If a 100-mg emergency dose has already been given, coordinate timing rather than blindly duplicate loading. This provides glucocorticoid and substantial mineralocorticoid activity. Dexamethasone does not replace the mineralocorticoid deficit. Oral tablets alone are inadequate with obstruction.

Restore circulating volume with isotonic crystalloid, using boluses and repeated assessment rather than a fixed large total in an elderly/cardiorenal patient. Add IV glucose for hypoglycaemia and provide ongoing substrate/monitoring. Treat dangerous hyperkalaemia using calcium if indicated, insulin–glucose with hypoglycaemia prevention, potassium removal and serial ECG/K checks. Correct severe sodium disturbance safely: reversal of cortisol deficiency can cause a water diuresis and unexpectedly rapid sodium rise. Treat sepsis, give appropriate antibiotics and arrange timely surgical source control.

## Anaesthesia and postoperative course

The bowel obstruction creates substantial aspiration and fluid-loss risk; plan decompression and airway protection according to urgency and airway assessment. Anticipate pronounced hypotension at induction; use titrated drugs, adequate vascular access, arterial monitoring when indicated and vasopressors alongside appropriate resuscitation/steroid replacement. Monitor perfusion, urine output, glucose, electrolytes and temperature. Avoid repeated empiric fluid loading for persistent vasodilatory shock without assessing cardiac function and congestion.

Postoperatively use HDU/ICU if unstable. Continue IV cover until haemodynamically stable and absorbing oral medication. Agree a stepped return to oral stress dosing and then maintenance with endocrine; do not abruptly discontinue replacement. High-dose hydrocortisone usually makes separate fludrocortisone unnecessary temporarily; resume the individual's mineralocorticoid regimen as hydrocortisone is reduced below stress levels and enteral absorption returns. Provide a clear handover, sick-day instructions, emergency steroid access and documentation before discharge.

**Sources and review basis:** Actual 2021.2 feedback reviewed; Society for Endocrinology adrenal-crisis guidance; perioperative steroid guidance and ESE/Endocrine Society 2024 recommendations, with primary versus glucocorticoid-induced disease distinguished.
rubric: Primary cortisol/aldosterone physiology and oral absorption problem (2).
Assessment, endocrine involvement, glucose/Na/K/volume and crisis recognition (2).
Correct IV hydrocortisone loading and ongoing replacement plus safe resuscitation/electrolyte management (4).
Anaesthetic risk, postoperative IV-to-oral transition and safe handover (2).

items.title: 2018.2 Q6: 2018.2 Q6 — Diabetes insipidus before trans-sphenoidal pituitary surge
items.q: 2018.2 Q6 — Diabetes insipidus before trans-sphenoidal pituitary surgery
items.model:
**Official question:** A patient scheduled for trans-sphenoidal pituitary surgery is noticed to have greater than normal urine output. How would you determine if this patient has diabetes insipidus? (30%) How would you manage diabetes insipidus in the perioperative period? (70%)

## Determine the diagnosis — 30%

Confirm true polyuria from a measured balance, usually >3 L/day in an adult or an abnormal weight-adjusted output, and distinguish urinary frequency from excessive volume. Ask about thirst, nocturia, intake, onset, drugs including lithium/diuretics, pituitary disease and prior treatment. Assess weight, haemodynamics, hydration and ability to access water; sodium can be normal when thirst and intake compensate.

Obtain paired serum sodium/osmolality and urine osmolality, plus glucose, renal function, potassium and calcium. AVP deficiency produces inappropriate hypotonic urine, commonly <300 mOsm/kg, despite high or rising plasma osmolality/sodium. Exclude glycosuric/osmotic diuresis, excessive administered fluids, diuretics, hypercalcaemia, hypokalaemia and recovery from obstruction/AKI. Establish whether this is central AVP deficiency or renal AVP resistance. In a stable uncertain case, endocrine-directed copeptin-based testing or supervised dynamic testing may be appropriate; do not perform water deprivation in an anaesthetised, dehydrated or hypernatraemic patient. A response to desmopressin supports central deficiency but is interpreted with the full clinical picture.

## Perioperative management — 70%

Agree an explicit plan with endocrine, anaesthesia, surgery and postoperative nursing/ICU. Record the patient's usual DDAVP formulation, route and response; avoid inadvertent omission when fasting, and prescribe an appropriate route conversion because oral, intranasal and IV doses are not equivalent. After nasal surgery intranasal absorption may be unreliable. Assess anterior pituitary function, particularly cortisol; hydrocortisone replacement can unmask previously concealed water loss.

Before surgery correct intravascular depletion with titrated isotonic crystalloid; then address free-water deficit and maintenance according to serum sodium and clinical status. If awake with intact thirst and swallowing, provide access to water and allow intake guided by thirst. If unable to drink, prescribe maintenance plus carefully assessed deficit/ongoing loss replacement, often enteral water or IV dextrose 5% after circulation is restored. Do not give unlimited free water after DDAVP-induced antidiuresis.

For established AVP deficiency with excessive dilute urine an example rescue dose is 1–2 micrograms DDAVP IV/IM under protocol, monitoring response before repeating. Do not prescribe a large fixed recurring IV dose without a review plan. Track hourly urine output and balance, serial weight, glucose and sodium, with sodium about every 2–4 h during active correction and less often once stable. Adjust to the observed trend rather than a formula alone.

After pituitary surgery anticipate early DI, a delayed antidiuretic/SIADH phase and possible permanent DI. Both **hypernatraemic dehydration and DDAVP/fluid-associated hyponatraemia** are important: the examiner explicitly highlighted hyponatraemia. With falling sodium or unexpectedly low output, reassess fluids and DDAVP immediately with endocrine. Avoid rapid correction of either chronic sodium disorder. Plan discharge education, thirst/intake advice, delayed sodium testing and urgent review symptoms; supply clear responsibility for DDAVP adjustment.

**Sources and review basis:** Actual 2018.2 feedback reviewed; endocrine inpatient AVP-deficiency guidance and pituitary sodium physiology. The official 30/70 split is preserved; educational marks are not the official analytic schedule.

**Signed-in sweep verification:** BJAEd pituitary surgery 2024 postoperative/endocrine sections confirm early DI surveillance and multidisciplinary hormonal/fluid planning. The article refers detailed sodium management to its dedicated sodium review; this model retains the broader triphasic and hyponatraemia safeguards from endocrine guidance.
rubric: Diagnosis: measured polyuria, paired osmolar pattern and alternatives/central versus renal mechanism (3).
Amount, type and speed of fluid; DDAVP strategy and close monitoring (3).
Postoperative triphasic course, hyponatraemia risk and discharge follow-up (2).

items.title: 2018.1 Q9: 2018.1 Q9 — Oliguria after laparotomy in an 80-year-old
items.q: 2018.1 Q9 — Oliguria after laparotomy in an 80-year-old
items.model:
**Official case:** An 80-year-old man is admitted to HDU after laparotomy for relief of large bowel obstruction. He has a urinary catheter; three hours later he remains oliguric. What are potential causes (50%) and how would you differentiate them (50%)?

## Causes

Use pre-renal, intrinsic and post-renal groups while checking for a simple measurement problem. A kinked/blocked catheter, closed clamp, disconnected tubing or retention must be excluded promptly despite a catheter being present.

Reduced renal perfusion may follow pre-existing dehydration from obstruction, vomiting, poor intake and bowel sequestration; unrecognised blood loss; anaesthetic vasodilatation; sepsis; reduced cardiac output from myocardial ischaemia/arrhythmia/failure; or increased intra-abdominal pressure. Venous congestion can reduce renal filtration even in a fluid-overloaded patient. Pain/stress-related ADH and sympathetic activation may cause transient oliguria without established structural AKI.

Intrinsic causes include ischaemic or septic tubular injury, pre-existing CKD, nephrotoxic exposure, pigment injury and less commonly interstitial or glomerular disease suggested by the history/urine. Post-renal causes include catheter obstruction, outlet disease and operative ureteric obstruction/injury; bilateral obstruction or a solitary functioning kidney makes ureteric injury especially consequential.

## Distinguishing causes

Confirm the hourly measured output against weight, duration and baseline; review the chart and inspect the catheter/bag, assess patency under local procedure and use bladder ultrasound. A full bladder suggests drainage/outflow failure. A small bladder does not exclude upper-tract obstruction.

Review preoperative creatinine and cardiac/renal/prostatic history, fasting/vomiting, perioperative balance, estimated blood loss, hypotension duration, anaesthetic record and drugs. Check current pressure and trend, heart rhythm, capillary refill, mental state, skin temperature, JVP, lung findings, oedema and abdominal distension/tenderness. Assess perfusion and congestion together. Use focused echo/ultrasound to answer a specific cardiac/volume question; CVP alone is not a reliable guide to fluid responsiveness.

Obtain haemoglobin, creatinine/urea/electrolytes, blood gas/lactate and glucose; compare serial values rather than await a creatinine rise. Perform urinalysis and, if appropriate, microscopy for blood/protein/casts and culture. Renal ultrasound assesses hydronephrosis when obstruction is plausible; early obstruction may not yet dilate the collecting system. Measure intra-abdominal pressure if abdominal compartment syndrome is suspected, and seek surgical review.

If history and examination support depletion, give a cautious titrated crystalloid challenge with an explicit response assessment; do not repeatedly give fluid solely to reach a urine target. Restore perfusion, treat haemorrhage/sepsis or cardiac dysfunction, relieve obstruction and review nephrotoxins. Diuretics can relieve congestion but do not diagnose or reverse tubular injury. FEna/FEurea have limitations in sepsis, CKD and diuretic use and must not overrule the clinical assessment. Persistent oliguria, severe electrolyte/acidaemic disturbance or pulmonary oedema warrants senior/renal/ICU escalation. An isolated three-hour period is concerning but does not, by duration alone, meet the six-hour KDIGO urine-output criterion.

**Sources and review basis:** Actual 2018.1 examiner report reviewed; KDIGO functional AKI definition and current perioperative renal assessment. This separate model preserves the 50/50 emphasis and is not a cross-reference to the 2012 answer.
rubric: Potential causes across pre-/intrinsic/post-renal groups, including catheter and operative context (5).
Logical differentiation: confirm output/drainage; history/record; perfusion and congestion examination; directed investigations and reassessment (5).

items.title: 2006.2 Q6: 2006.2 Q6 — Electrolyte abnormalities of chronic renal failure
items.q: 2006.2 Q6 — Electrolyte abnormalities of chronic renal failure
items.model:
**Official question:** List and explain the typical electrolyte abnormalities of chronic renal failure.

The pattern depends on CKD severity, residual urine output, diet, medications and dialysis. Results are not all necessarily abnormal in every patient. Explain impaired homeostasis rather than provide an unqualified list, and stay within electrolytes as requested.

**Potassium:** Hyperkalaemia becomes more likely as functioning nephron mass, distal sodium delivery and aldosterone-dependent potassium secretion become inadequate. Hyporeninaemic hypoaldosteronism, RAAS inhibitors, potassium-sparing drugs, supplements, acidosis and tissue breakdown increase risk. Adaptation and gastrointestinal excretion can maintain a normal concentration until advanced disease. Conversely, diuretics, poor intake or dialysis can cause hypokalaemia; CKD does not make a high potassium inevitable. Severe hyperkalaemia can cause conduction disturbance and lethal arrhythmia.

**Sodium and water:** Serum sodium reflects the relationship between exchangeable solute and body water, not total-body sodium alone. Reduced GFR limits excretion of a sodium load, so extracellular sodium/water retention, hypertension and oedema may coexist with a normal serum sodium. Impaired dilution plus excess hypotonic intake can cause dilutional hyponatraemia; impaired concentrating ability and inadequate access to water can contribute to hypernatraemia. Do not state that all chronic renal failure causes hypernatraemia or that oedema proves a high serum sodium.

**Phosphate:** Reduced filtered load and excretory capacity ultimately produce phosphate retention and hyperphosphataemia, although compensatory FGF23/PTH can keep the serum result normal earlier. Dialysis, phosphate binders and intake alter the measured value. Hypophosphataemia can occur with poor intake, treatment or refeeding.

**Calcium:** Reduced renal calcitriol production impairs intestinal calcium absorption; phosphate retention also contributes to low ionised calcium. Hypocalcaemia and reduced calcitriol stimulate secondary hyperparathyroidism, which increases bone turnover. Thus elevated PTH is generally compensatory rather than the primary explanation for low calcium. In advanced autonomous/tertiary hyperparathyroidism, or during calcium/vitamin-D treatment, calcium may be high. Interpret ionised calcium where albumin, pH or critical illness make corrected total calcium unreliable. CKD mineral-bone disease includes a calcium–phosphate–PTH interaction, not invariably a fixed low-calcium result.

**Magnesium:** Renal magnesium excretion falls in advanced failure, especially with magnesium-containing antacids/laxatives or administered magnesium, producing hypermagnesaemia. Earlier CKD or dialysis/diuretic/GI losses may instead give a normal or low value. Significant elevation suppresses neuromuscular and cardiovascular function.

**Bicarbonate/chloride:** Reduced ammonium generation and net acid excretion cause metabolic acidosis with reduced bicarbonate. Earlier disease can be predominantly normal-gap/hyperchloraemic; accumulated unmeasured anions contribute in advanced uraemia. Vomiting, alkali or dialysis can change this pattern. Do not substitute a long account of uraemia, anaemia, creatinine elevation or drug accumulation for the electrolyte answer: the examiner awarded no marks for unrelated biochemical abnormalities.

**Sources and review basis:** Actual 2006.2 examiner commentary reviewed. KDIGO 2024 CKD guidance; renal physiology; BJAEd CKD/anaesthesia 2022 identified as background, not freshly read in full. The pass rate is 45% in the report summary table; the individual question commentary omits it.
rubric: Potassium abnormality, impaired excretion and modifying factors (2).
Serum sodium versus total-body sodium/water distinction (2).
Phosphate retention and calcium–calcitriol–PTH physiology, with exceptions (3).
Bicarbonate/acidosis explanation and strict electrolyte focus (2).

items.title: 2007.2 Q12: 2007.2 Q12 — Pyloric stenosis: biochemistry and fluid resuscitation
items.q: 2007.2 Q12 — Pyloric stenosis: biochemistry and fluid resuscitation
items.model:
**Official case:** A three-week-old term male infant has had projectile vomiting for two weeks and weighs 2.8 kg, from birth weight 3.1 kg. Presumed pyloric stenosis; Na 129, K 3.0, Cl 84, HCO3 36 mmol/L; creatinine 69 (unit corrupted in the text extraction; clinically interpret as micromol/L after checking the laboratory report), glucose 3.0 mmol/L. Explain the abnormalities, describe appropriate fluid resuscitation, and list laboratory criteria for proceeding to surgery. The report says the first two sections carried more weight, but provides no exact percentage split.

## Mechanisms

Gastric loss removes hydrogen, chloride, sodium, water and some potassium, producing hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis and dehydration. Initial bicarbonaturia can increase urinary sodium, potassium and water loss. With worsening extracellular depletion, renal perfusion falls and proximal sodium/bicarbonate reabsorption rises. RAAS activation increases distal sodium retention at the expense of potassium and hydrogen loss, maintaining alkalosis. Total-body potassium depletion is greater than the serum measurement alone suggests; severe depletion and chloride deficiency contribute to paradoxical aciduria despite systemic alkalosis.

Non-osmotic ADH release from depletion/stress, together with sodium loss and inappropriate water replacement, contributes to hyponatraemia. Fasting and low glycogen reserves create hypoglycaemia risk even if glucose 3.0 is within the printed interval. Creatinine needs neonatal reference/timing and hydration context; do not label advanced renal failure from this value alone. The weight is about 10% below birth weight, but birth-to-current change in a three-week-old is not an exact measure of the current deficit because expected growth, early physiological loss and intake also matter. Assess the infant, not just the arithmetic.

## Fluid resuscitation

This is usually a correction-before-pyloromyotomy problem. Obtain paediatric/surgical help, weigh, assess perfusion, fontanelle, mucosa, skin turgor and urine output; establish IV access and monitor cardiorespiratory state, temperature and glucose. Keep nil by mouth and use appropriate gastric decompression with measured replacement of ongoing losses.

If shocked, give titrated isotonic saline, for example 10 mL/kg (28 mL), reassess and repeat according to the local neonatal pathway. The historical examiner accepted 20-mL/kg boluses; current practice emphasises reassessment and avoiding unnecessary large rapid volumes. Use an isotonic chloride-containing maintenance/deficit regimen with appropriate glucose to prevent fasting hypoglycaemia. Potassium, commonly within a 20–40-mmol/L protocolised range, is added only after checking concentration, renal function and established urine output; never give an IV potassium bolus. Prescribe deficit, maintenance and measured losses separately, avoiding double counting, and adjust to serial weight, output and blood results. A fixed 1.5-times-maintenance rate is an example pathway, not a universal requirement for every infant.

## Proceeding criteria

Demonstrate clinical rehydration, adequate perfusion/output, stable glucose and correction of chloride-responsive alkalosis and important sodium/potassium derangements before surgery. State the local paediatric thresholds, commonly bicarbonate <28–30 mmol/L with chloride in the normal range and acceptable sodium/potassium; these are pathway examples, not universal ANZCA numerical standards. The **2007 examiner specifically prioritised chloride/bicarbonate correction**, cited chloride ≥105 mmol/L for most infants to have no residual alkalosis, and accepted urine chloride >20 plus sodium/potassium discussion for additional credit. Preserve this as historical report teaching rather than insist every current pathway must use the same number. CSF alkalosis can lag blood correction; plan postoperative apnoea monitoring and do not assume a corrected serum value eliminates respiratory risk.

**Sources and review basis:** Actual 2007.2 Q12 OCR commentary reviewed; contemporary paediatric fluid/resuscitation principles and BJAEd acid–base mechanisms. This is a separate historical question, not an invented variant of 2022.2 Q15.
rubric: Mechanism: gastric losses, renal maintenance of alkalosis, ADH/Na and total-body K deficit (4).
Weight/clinical assessment, explicit isotonic chloride/glucose resuscitation, safe K and ongoing-loss plan (4).
Clinical recovery and justified laboratory targets, distinguishing historical report from current local pathway (2).
